steps.q: What does a load balancer do?
choices: Keeps copies of the latest answers
Makes the database run faster
Checks every user's password
Spreads requests across the servers
steps.why: It spreads requests so no single server takes all the work.

steps.q: What does a cache save?
choices: The cost of running the servers
Repeat trips to the database
The time spent writing new code
The load balancer's work
steps.why: It remembers recent answers, so the database is asked less often.

steps.q: Why can a sudden spike still hurt even with autoscaling?
choices: Servers can never be scaled up
The database switches itself off
New servers take minutes to start
The load balancer forgets the servers
steps.why: Autoscaling reacts after load rises, and starting servers takes a few minutes.

takeaway: A system is a few boxes in a line, and design is deciding which boxes and how many. Count first: the first practice problem, a URL shortener at about 5,000 requests a second, needs about 6 servers, not 3 (approx.).

title: What a request is, and p50 versus p99
summary: A request is one question and one answer. Averages hide the slow ones that people remember.

steps.title: One tap, one request
steps.text: A request is one question from a person ("show my feed") and one answer. Every request waits a little. Latency is that wait, in milliseconds (ms). A blink is about 100 ms (approx.).

steps.title: p50 and p99
steps.text: p50 is the wait that half of requests beat, the typical one. p99 is the wait that 99 of every 100 requests beat, so the slowest 1 in 100 is slower than that. If a page makes 10 requests, about 1 page in 10 meets a p99 request, so p99 is what people feel.

steps.prompt: People in Europe wait too long. Follow the whole request path: move both the app servers and their database to Europe so no request crosses the ocean.
steps.hint: Select the server and the database, then set Region to Europe. The trip across the ocean and back adds about 80 ms (approx.).

rows.label: Europe to Asia Pacific and back

steps.q: What is p99?
choices: The average wait across every request
The wait the fastest 1 in 100 saw
The wait 99 of 100 requests beat
The wait of the single slowest request
steps.why: The slowest 1 in 100 requests is slower than p99.

steps.q: Why watch p99 and not just the average?
choices: The p99 is far cheaper to measure
A few very slow requests spoil a page
The average is always wrong by half
Users only ever read the p99 figure
steps.why: A page makes many requests, so slow ones show up often for real people.

steps.q: How do you cut the wait for far-away users?
choices: Add more memory to every server
Turn off all logging for a day
Compress the logo image more
Put the service closer to them
steps.why: Distance sets a floor on latency that no faster server can beat.

takeaway: Judge a system by its slow requests, and remember distance is part of latency.

title: Numbers you can do in your head
summary: Turn monthly users into requests per second and servers needed, with a pencil.

steps.title: Start with people
steps.text: Say 30 million people use your app a month and each visit makes 20 requests. Not everyone visits daily; a third do, so 10 million visitors a day. That is 200 million requests a day (all numbers approx.).

steps.title: Divide by a day, then by the peak
steps.text: A day has about 86,400 seconds; call it 100,000. 200 million divided by 100,000 is 2,000 requests a second on average. Peak hour is often 3 times the average, so plan for about 6,000 a second.

steps.prompt: Peak is 9,000 requests a second. Serve it with at least 25% spare app capacity.
steps.hint: One server handles about 1,000 requests a second (approx.). Divide the peak by that capacity, then leave at least 25% spare for a slow server or a small burst.

rows.label: 1 million requests a day at 2 KB each

steps.q: About how many seconds are in a day, for quick math?
steps.why: It is 86,400, and 100,000 is close enough to divide by in your head.

steps.q: Average load is 2,000 requests a second. Peak is often about:
choices: About the same as the average
About half of the average
About 3 times the average
About 100 times the average
steps.why: Traffic bunches into busy hours; 2 to 4 times the average is common (approx.).

steps.q: One server handles 1,000 requests a second and you need 9,000. How many do you run?
choices: Exactly 9
About 5
About 90
About 12
steps.why: Leave headroom for spikes and for servers being replaced.

takeaway: Divide by 100,000 for a day, multiply by 3 for the peak, and leave headroom.

title: Spreading load
summary: A load balancer hands each request to a free server so none is overwhelmed.

steps.title: One address, many servers
steps.text: People type one address. Behind it you can run many servers, but something must choose which one answers. That is the load balancer. It also notices a broken server and stops sending it work.

steps.prompt: This demo sends about 2,550 requests a second overnight and 3,000/s at the daytime peak, with small traffic fluctuations. Retries are off. One size M server handles ≈ 1,000/s. Add a load balancer and set App servers to 5 for headroom.

between.note: The load balancer goes between the phone and the servers, so it can share requests out. Drop it onto that line.

steps.hint: Drag Load balancer between the phone and the servers, then set App servers to 5 at size M. At peak, 3,000 ÷ (1,000 × 70%) ≈ 4.3, rounded up to 5 servers.

steps.title: Choosing who is next
steps.text: Round robin deals requests out in turn, like cards. Least requests picks the server with the fewest in progress. Least requests is better when some requests are slow.

rows.label: Health check every
rows.how: a dead server is dropped within a minute, approx.

rows.label: Servers for this demo
rows.how: 3,000 requests/s ÷ (1,000 requests/s per server × 70% busy) ≈ 4.3, rounded up to 5.

steps.q: What does a load balancer do when one server dies?
choices: Sends it even more work
Waits until it comes back
Restarts the database
Stops sending it new requests
steps.why: Health checks find the broken server and traffic goes to the others.

steps.q: Which setting suits requests of very different lengths?
choices: Round robin, one server after another
Random, picking any server it likes
Fixed, always the very first server
Least requests, the freest server
steps.why: Least requests keeps long jobs from piling onto one server.

steps.q: Can a load balancer be a single point of failure?
choices: Never, because it is built to be safe
Yes, unless it runs in several places
Only when it runs in the cloud
Only when it has too few servers
steps.why: Managed balancers span several zones for exactly this reason.

takeaway: A load balancer lets many servers act as one, and hides the ones that fail.

title: Remembering answers
summary: A cache keeps recent answers in memory so the database is asked less.

steps.title: The same question again
steps.text: Most people ask for the same few things: today's top stories, a popular profile. Asking the database each time repeats work. A cache keeps the last answer in fast memory and hands it back.

steps.prompt: The database is nearly full. Repeated answers may be at most 60 seconds old. Reduce its load while keeping that freshness limit.

between.note: A cache helps most between the servers and the database, so the servers ask it first. Drop it onto the line between them.

steps.hint: Drag Cache from the Data stores group onto the line from the servers to the database.

steps.title: Fresh versus fast
steps.text: A cache entry has a time to live (TTL), how long it is kept. A long TTL means more hits but older answers. A short TTL means fresher answers but more trips to the database.

steps.q: A cache answers 90 percent of questions. How much work reaches the database?
choices: About 90 percent of it
About half of it
About 10 percent of it
None of it at all
steps.why: Only the misses go through.

steps.q: What is the cost of a long TTL?
choices: It costs more money to run
Answers may be out of date
It means fewer cache hits
It slows the database down
steps.why: The cache can hand back something that has since changed.

steps.q: Which data suits caching best?
choices: Written once and never read again
Different for every single request
Private to one user each time
Read often and changes rarely
steps.why: Reused answers are where the savings are.

takeaway: A cache trades a little freshness for a lot of speed and a calmer database.

title: Copies near users
summary: A CDN keeps copies of files and pages close to people, so your servers see far fewer requests.

steps.title: Do not cross the world for a picture
steps.text: Pictures, videos and pages that look the same for everyone can be copied to many small sites near people. That network of copies is a content delivery network (CDN). The nearest copy answers; your own servers are asked only when the copy is missing.

steps.prompt: Twenty thousand people a second want the same pages. Protect your servers with a CDN.

between.note: A CDN sits between the browser and the servers, so pages are answered close to the visitor. Drop it onto that line.

steps.hint: Drag CDN between the browser and the servers.

rows.label: Typical CDN hit rate for static files
Sending data out to the internet

steps.q: What does a CDN hold?
choices: Your users' passwords for safe keeping
A full working copy of your database
The code your servers run on
Copies of files and pages near users
steps.why: It keeps copies near people.

steps.q: Which content is a poor fit for a CDN?
choices: A logo shown on every page of the site
A video that millions of people watch
A user's own bank balance
A style sheet shared by every page
steps.why: Private data that differs per person should not be shared copies.

steps.q: What happens on a CDN miss?
choices: The request fails and the user retries
The CDN asks the user for the file
It goes to your servers, then is kept
The page is shown blank for a while
steps.why: The edge fetches from your origin, then keeps the copy for the next person.

takeaway: Put copies of shared content near people; keep your servers for what only they can do.

title: Adding servers, and why it is late
summary: Autoscaling adds servers when busy, but new servers take minutes to start.

steps.title: More servers on demand
steps.text: Evening traffic is much heavier than the dead of night. Instead of paying for peak servers all day, autoscaling adds servers when they are busy and removes them when quiet.

steps.prompt: Evening rush and a viral spike are coming. Turn on Autoscale for the servers.
steps.hint: Select the servers, switch Autoscale on, and set the highest number to 20 with a target of 60 percent.

steps.title: Why it is always a little late
steps.text: Autoscaling reacts after load rises, and a new server needs 2 to 4 minutes to start (approx.). A steep spike can break things before help arrives. Keep spare room, or scale before a known event.

steps.q: Why not run peak servers all day?
choices: Servers wear out faster when always on
You pay for servers that sit idle
The law limits server running hours
Peak servers are slower at night
steps.why: Autoscaling saves money in quiet hours.

steps.q: Why can a spike still break an autoscaled system?
choices: Autoscaling is switched off after dark
Servers cannot be added during a spike
New servers need minutes to start up
The load balancer refuses extra servers
steps.why: The spike can outrun the startup time.

steps.q: A famous launch is at noon. Best move?
choices: Wait and let autoscaling react to it
Turn off the cache to save money now
Ask users to come back a bit later
Add servers a little before noon
steps.why: When you know the time, scale ahead of it.

takeaway: Autoscaling follows the crowd; for known surges, scale ahead of it.

title: Copies are a little behind
summary: Read copies share the load, but they trail the original by a moment.

steps.title: Many readers, one writer
steps.text: A busy database can keep copies called replicas. All changes go to the primary, which sends them on. Replicas answer reads, so one database becomes many. With asynchronous replication, changes arrive later, so a replica can be slightly out of date.

steps.prompt: Keep App servers connected to SQL database for writes. Place Read replica beside the database, then connect SQL database to Read replica to copy changes. Next, connect App servers to Read replica for reads. Select Read replica and set its replica count to 4 at size M. At peak, 8,280 reads/s share 5 copies, each handling ≈ 8,000 reads/s; 720 writes/s stay on the primary at ≈ 2,000 writes/s capacity. Primary busy is ≈ 36% writes + 21% reads = 57%. Keep it below 70 percent for a simulated minute.
steps.hint: A dropped replica needs two links: SQL database → Read replica copies changes; App servers → Read replica carries reads. Keep App servers → SQL database. At peak, 9,000 × 92% = 8,280 reads/s and 9,000 × 8% = 720 writes/s. At size M, the primary handles ≈ 8,000 reads/s or ≈ 2,000 writes/s. Writes alone use 720 ÷ 2,000 = 36%. This model shares reads by capacity across the primary and replicas. With 4 replicas, the primary gets about one fifth of reads: 8,280 ÷ 5 ÷ 8,000 ≈ 21%. Total primary load is ≈ 36% + 21% = 57%, leaving room below 70%. Select Read replica and set its replica count to 4, keeping both databases at size M.

steps.title: Stale on purpose
steps.text: Replication is usually asynchronous: the primary says "done" without waiting for replicas to acknowledge the change. That is fast, but a read right after your own write can show the old value. Normal lag is about 100 ms (approx.); in trouble it can reach many seconds. Synchronous replication waits for the required replicas to acknowledge before confirming a write, adding latency. Whether a replica can serve that write immediately depends on whether its acknowledgement means received, durably stored or applied.

rows.label: Primary load with 4 replicas
rows.how: 720 writes/s ÷ 2,000 + (8,280 reads/s ÷ 5 copies) ÷ 8,000 ≈ 36% + 21%. Keep the app-to-primary write link and both replica links.

rows.label: Writes
rows.how: replicas do not add write capacity

steps.q: Where do writes go with read replicas?
choices: Any replica, whichever is nearest
A random replica each time
The cache layer in front
The primary, then copied on
steps.why: Replicas copy the primary and cannot take writes.

steps.q: You post a comment and refresh. It is missing. Likely cause?
choices: The server you used was deleted
The CDN is switched off
The replica was a moment behind
Comments are never saved
steps.why: Reading from a lagging replica returns slightly old data.

steps.q: Do replicas add write capacity?
choices: Yes, almost in a straight line
No, they only add reads
Only if a cache sits in front
Yes, once you add ten of them
steps.why: Every write still has to be applied by the primary.

takeaway: Replicas scale reads. Asynchronous replicas can lag behind the primary; synchronous replication waits for the required acknowledgements before confirming a write, trading latency for stronger guarantees.

title: Splitting data
summary: When one database cannot take the writes, split the data across several.

steps.title: One database has a ceiling
steps.text: A single database can only take so many writes, and replicas do not help. Sharding splits the data by a key, such as user id, so each shard holds a slice and takes only its share of writes.

steps.prompt: Writes are far above what one database can do. Swap it for a sharded database.
steps.hint: Remove the single database, place Sharded SQL, connect the servers to it, and set Units to 4 or more.

steps.title: Choosing the key
steps.text: A good key spreads people evenly, like a user id. A bad key piles them up, like a country with half your users. Questions across all shards, such as "everyone named Sam", are slower because every shard must answer.

rows.label: Four shards
rows.how: if the key spreads evenly, approx.

steps.q: Sharding mainly helps with:
choices: Making each single query much faster
Cutting the monthly bill by a half
Keeping all the data in one place
Handling more writes and more data
steps.why: Each shard handles only a slice of the writes and the data.

steps.q: Which is the best shard key?
choices: The user's country
A hash of the user id
The day of the week
The month of sign-up
steps.why: User ids spread evenly; countries and days pile up.

steps.q: What gets harder after sharding?
choices: Reading one user's own records
Writing a single new row
Looking up one record by its key
Questions that span many shards
steps.why: They must visit every shard and combine the answers.

takeaway: Shard when writes or size outgrow one machine, and pick a key that spreads evenly.

title: When one item is popular
summary: Sharding spreads keys, not popularity. One star item can still overload one shard.

steps.title: The celebrity problem
steps.text: Shards split keys evenly, but not attention. If one post goes viral, every request for it lands on the one shard that holds it. That shard melts while the others sit idle.

steps.prompt: One item gets a third of all reads. Protect the shards with a cache.

between.note: The cache has to sit between the servers and the database, so the popular item is answered from memory. Drop it onto that line.

steps.hint: Place a Cache between the servers and the database so the popular item is answered from memory.

steps.title: Ways out
steps.text: Cache the hot item so the shard is rarely asked. Keep several copies of it. Or split the key, for example by adding a small number to the end, and combine the pieces on read.

rows.label: A hot item with 30 percent of reads
rows.value: ≈ 2.5 times a fair share on its shard
rows.how: its shard carries 30 + 70 ÷ 6 ≈ 42 percent of reads, against a fair 16.7 percent: 42 ÷ 16.7 ≈ 2.5

steps.q: Does adding shards fix a hot key?
choices: Yes, more shards always spread it out
Only if you also turn replicas off
Yes, once you add ten more shards
No, that key still sits on one shard
steps.why: The hot key is still stored in one place.

steps.q: Which is a good fix?
choices: Lower the timeout on every call
Add a second database just for writes
Keep a cached copy of the hot item
Send the hot item to every shard
steps.why: A cache answers most requests without touching the shard.

steps.q: Why do hot keys surprise teams?
choices: Small tests always catch them first
Hot keys cannot be measured in a log
They only show up in the night hours
The average load looks perfectly fine
steps.why: Overall utilisation is low while one shard is overwhelmed.

takeaway: Spread keys with shards and spread attention with caches and copies.

title: Search is a copy
summary: A search index is a second copy of your data, shaped for finding words fast.

steps.title: Looking up is not searching
steps.text: A database finds a row by its id quickly. Finding every row that mentions "red shoes" is a different job. A search index keeps a word-to-document map built just for that, and it is a copy, kept up to date by a feed of changes.

steps.prompt: Search is crushing the database. Move it to a search index and keep the index fed.
steps.hint: Place a Search index and connect the servers to it. Then add a Change feed from the database to the index.

steps.title: Slightly behind again
steps.text: The index is updated after the database changes, so a brand new item can take a second or more to become searchable (approx.). The database stays the source of truth; the index can be rebuilt from it.

rows.label: Index size versus data
rows.how: depends on what you index, approx.

steps.q: Which is the source of truth?
choices: The search index built from them
The cache in front of the database
The main database of records
The log of recent queries
steps.why: The index is a rebuildable copy.

steps.q: You add an item and cannot find it for a second. Why?
choices: Search is broken until someone restarts it
The item was lost on its way in
The index updates a moment later
Items always need a full day to show
steps.why: Changes reach the index after they reach the database.

steps.q: Why not use the database for all search?
choices: Databases cannot store long pieces of text
It is against the rules at larger companies
Matching words in millions of rows is slow
Search needs a different kind of language
steps.why: Indexes are built for exactly that job.

takeaway: Keep one source of truth and feed purpose-built copies for search.

title: Hot, warm, cold and archive
summary: Old data is rarely read, so keep it somewhere cheaper and slower.

steps.title: Not all data is equal
steps.text: Yesterday's photos are viewed all the time; photos from five years ago almost never. Fast storage costs more per gigabyte. Move data down tiers as it ages: hot for now, warm for this month, cold for rarely, archive for the law.

steps.prompt: You hold 120 TB and most of it is old. Move it to cheaper storage to cut the bill.
steps.hint: Place a Cold archive, connect the storage to it, and shorten how long the main storage keeps data.

rows.label: Archive
rows.how: minutes to hours to get back, approx.

steps.q: What do you give up for cheaper storage?
choices: The safety of the stored data
The ability to ever delete it
How fast you get data back
Nothing at all
steps.why: Cold and archive tiers cost less but take longer to read.

steps.q: A law says keep invoices 7 years but nobody reads them. Which tier?
choices: The hot tier, for quick reads
Delete them after one year
The archive tier, which is cheap
A cache next to the servers
steps.why: You must keep them cheaply and rarely read them.

steps.q: Who should decide when data moves down a tier?
choices: Someone moving it by hand weekly
Nobody, it should never move
The newest engineer on the team
A rule that goes by the age
steps.why: Lifecycle rules do it automatically.

takeaway: Match storage to how often data is read, and move it down as it ages.

title: Waiting instead of breaking
summary: A queue lets a burst wait in line instead of crashing the thing behind it.

steps.title: A line at the bakery
steps.text: If work arrives faster than it can be done, you can drop it or make it wait. A queue is the line. The sender says "got it" at once, and workers take items at their own pace. Waiting is better than breaking, as long as the line does not grow forever.

steps.prompt: A burst of writes is more than the database can take. Put a queue and workers in front of it. Acceptance means the queue took the job, not that it finished. Completion lag shows the oldest waiting job; expiry risk compares its age with the job deadline. The model tracks traffic as rates rather than individual jobs.
steps.hint: Place a Queue and Background workers, so the path is servers, queue, workers, database. Then give the workers enough units for the normal 1,500 writes a second (about 10, at about 200 jobs a second each, approx.), or the line grows all day and work waits past its limit. The size M database handles ≈ 2,000 writes/s, so adding workers beyond that cannot raise completed drain. The burst brings ≈ 4,500 writes/s: the queue must wait for arrivals to fall, or you must increase database capacity or slow senders.

steps.title: Backpressure
steps.text: If the line keeps growing, the system must push back: slow senders, say "try later", or drop the least important work. Without it, the queue fills up and delays grow until the data is stale.

rows.label: Backlog of 1 million at 2,000 a second
1,500 arrivals and 2,000 completed a second
rows.how: Net drain is service minus arrivals: 2,000 - 1,500 = 500 jobs a second. Time to clear = backlog / (service rate - arrival rate), so 1,000,000 / (2,000 - 1,500) / 60 ≈ 33.3 minutes. At equal rates the backlog stays; with more arrivals it grows.

steps.q: What does a queue buy you?
choices: More capacity for the database
Time to catch up after a burst
Perfect order for every message
Faster answers to every user
steps.why: It smooths bursts; it does not add capacity.

steps.q: The queue grows all day and never shrinks. What now?
choices: Nothing, queues can grow forever
Delete the queue and start fresh
Buy a bigger database server
Add workers or slow the senders
steps.why: Work is arriving faster than it is done; either side must change.

steps.q: What is backpressure?
choices: A database setting that caps how large a row can be
Telling senders to ease off as the line grows
A kind of cache that clears older entries early
A copy of the queue kept in a second region
steps.why: It stops overload from growing without end.

takeaway: Queues turn spikes into waiting; backpressure stops the waiting from growing forever.

title: One post, millions of feeds
summary: A post by a celebrity must reach millions of feeds; do it in the background.

steps.title: Write once, read once, or both
steps.text: When someone posts, followers must see it. Fan-out on write copies the post into every follower's feed now, so reading is fast. Fan-out on read leaves it alone and builds the feed when someone opens the app. Celebrities with 20 million followers make the first approach very heavy.

steps.prompt: A celebrity post makes 25 times the writes. Absorb it with a queue and workers.
steps.hint: Put a Queue and Worker pool on the write path so the copies are made in the background.

steps.title: A mix
steps.text: Big systems mix both: copy into feeds for everyday accounts, and for celebrities merge their latest posts in when the feed is read.

steps.q: Fan-out on write makes:
choices: Reading slow and writing light
Reading fast and writing heavy
Both reading and writing light
Both reading and writing heavy
steps.why: The work is done at post time.

steps.q: Why queue the copying?
choices: Queues make every copy arrive faster
Copies must be made one at a time
The poster should not wait on copies
Queues are free, so they cost nothing
steps.why: The post is accepted at once and delivered over the next seconds.

steps.q: How do big feeds treat celebrities?
choices: Copy their posts like anyone's
Hide them from every feed
Give each fan a private copy first
Merge their posts in at read time
steps.why: It avoids millions of writes per post.

takeaway: Do heavy fan-out in the background, and treat huge accounts differently.

title: Live sockets and presence
summary: Chat and live scores keep a connection open; that changes how you count capacity.

steps.title: Open lines
steps.text: Normal web requests ask and leave. A live feature, like chat, keeps a connection open so the server can push messages the moment they happen. A server can hold tens of thousands of open lines (approx.), but each one uses memory even when quiet.

steps.prompt: Chat messages overwhelm the app servers. Add a websocket gateway to hold the connections.

between.note: The gateway goes between the phones and the servers, so it holds the open connections. Drop it onto that line.

steps.hint: Place a Websocket gateway between the phones and the servers.

steps.title: Who is online
steps.text: Presence ("Sam is online") is a stream of tiny updates. Keep it in memory, expire it fast, and accept that it is a little off. Do not write it to the main database.

steps.q: Why is a live feature costly when users are quiet?
choices: Messages are very large in size
They always need a CDN in front
Idle connections still hold memory
Every quiet user needs a database
steps.why: Each idle connection still takes a slot.

steps.q: Where should "online now" be stored?
choices: In the main database forever
In memory with a short expiry
In a long-term archive
In a printed log file
steps.why: It changes constantly and is only useful for a moment.

steps.q: A gateway server restarts. What happens to its users?
choices: Nothing, the users never notice
Their messages vanish for good
They are moved to another user
They reconnect, all at once
steps.why: Reconnect with random delay so they do not stampede.

takeaway: Count open connections, not just requests, and keep presence light.

title: Which copy is the truth
summary: With several copies, you choose between always-latest and always-fast.

steps.title: Two copies, two answers
steps.text: With a primary and a replica, two people can read different values for a moment. Strong consistency means every read sees the latest write, and costs a little speed. Eventual consistency means copies catch up soon, and is faster and cheaper.

steps.prompt: Users must see their own edits at once. Make writes safe and read the latest from the primary.
steps.hint: Set the database Replication to sync so no write is lost. For reads that must be current, send them to the primary, not the replica.

steps.title: Choose per screen
steps.text: You do not have to pick one for the whole app. A bank balance and a "payment sent" screen need the latest. A like count or a view counter can be a few seconds late. Use the expensive guarantee only where it matters.

rows.label: Sync write to a second copy

steps.q: Strong consistency means:
choices: Reads are always the fastest possible
Data is always encrypted on disk
Writes can never fail
Reads see the latest write
steps.why: It never shows you an older value than the last write.

steps.q: Which screen can be eventually consistent?
choices: Account balance after a transfer
A like counter
A seat that was just booked
A payment that was just made
steps.why: Nobody is harmed if a like count is a few seconds old.

steps.q: What does sync replication protect against?
choices: Slow queries when many users read at once
Losing a saved write if the primary dies
Sudden traffic spikes at the busiest hour
Cache entries going out of date too soon
steps.why: The write exists on two machines before you are told it worked.

takeaway: Pick the strongest guarantee only where being wrong would hurt.

title: Exactly once, on purpose
summary: Retries are normal, so every action must be safe to repeat.

steps.title: Did my payment go through?
steps.text: Networks drop answers. A phone taps Pay, the payment succeeds, the reply is lost, and the app tries again. Without care the customer is charged twice. A retry is safe only if repeating the action has the same effect as doing it once. That property is called idempotency.

steps.prompt: The queue delivers some payments twice, and customers are charged twice. Add an idempotency store.
steps.hint: Place an Idempotency store beside the workers and connect the workers to it. Each payment carries a unique key; a repeated key returns the first result.

steps.title: The key
steps.text: The app makes one random key per purchase and sends it with every try. The server checks the key first: seen before, return the saved answer; new, do the work and save it. Keys are kept for a day or more (approx.).

steps.q: What is an idempotent action?
choices: Guaranteed to finish very quickly
Safe to run twice, same result
Always stored in a fast cache
Only allowed to run a single time
steps.why: Doing it twice has the same effect as once.

steps.q: Why do duplicates happen with queues?
choices: Queues are broken and lose count
Servers copy messages on purpose
Clocks drift between the servers
A message may be delivered twice
steps.why: If an acknowledgement is lost, the message is delivered again.

steps.q: Where does the idempotency key come from?
choices: The database, new for each retry
The client, once per action
The CDN, at the edge
The load balancer, per server
steps.why: The same key must travel with every retry of one action.

takeaway: Give every action a key, and repeating it becomes harmless.

title: Saying "slow down" politely
summary: A limit per client stops one noisy caller or a flood from taking everyone down.

steps.title: A bouncer, not a wall
steps.text: One buggy script or an attacker can send more requests than the whole crowd. A rate limiter counts requests per client and answers the extra ones with a quick "too many requests" (HTTP 429). Everyone else is served as usual.

steps.prompt: A flood of junk traffic is hitting the servers. Add a rate limiter in front.

between.note: The limiter goes in front of the servers, between the browser and them, so junk is stopped early. Drop it onto that line.

steps.hint: Place a Rate limiter between the browser and the servers. Try a limit of 100 requests per second per client.

steps.title: How it counts
steps.text: A token bucket gives each client tokens that refill at a steady rate; each request spends one. A short burst is fine, a long flood runs dry. If the limiter itself is down you choose: fail open (let everyone in) or fail closed (let nobody in).

rows.label: Typical API limit
rows.value: ≈ 1 to 100 requests a second per key
rows.how: free public tiers are often about 5,000 an hour (1.4 a second); paid tiers far more, approx.

steps.q: What does a rate limiter send back to an over-limit client?
choices: The data anyway, only slower
A 500 server error and an apology
Nothing, so the client waits forever
A 429 "too many requests" reply
steps.why: A fast, polite refusal.

steps.q: If the limiter fails, "fail open" means:
choices: Block everyone until it recovers
Restart all the servers at once
Let requests through for now
Send every request to a queue
steps.why: Open favors availability; closed favors protection.

steps.q: Why limit per client, not just in total?
choices: It is far easier to build and to run
One client cannot eat everyone's share
Totals cannot be counted across servers
It makes every request run faster
steps.why: A total cap punishes everyone for one bad caller.

takeaway: Limit each caller so one flood cannot become everyone's outage.

title: Timeouts and failing fast
summary: When a dependency is slow, give up early so your servers do not pile up waiting.

steps.title: A slow friend is worse than a dead one
steps.text: A dead service fails fast. A slow one holds your servers waiting until they have no room for anything else. Set a timeout so you stop waiting after a short time, and add a circuit breaker that stops calling a failing service for a while and answers from a fallback.

steps.prompt: The map service has become slow and is dragging everything down. Add a timeout and a circuit breaker.

between.note: The breaker goes between the servers and the map service, so a slow map cannot drag the servers down. Drop it onto that line.

steps.hint: Set the servers' Timeout to 300 ms and place a Circuit breaker between the servers and the map service.

steps.title: Open, closed, half open
steps.text: A closed breaker lets calls through. After too many failures it opens: calls fail at once, with a fallback such as "map unavailable". After about 30 seconds it half-opens to test one call, and closes if it works.

rows.label: A good timeout
rows.how: for example 300 ms if p99 is 100 ms

steps.q: Why is a slow service worse than a dead one?
choices: Slow services cost much more to run
Dead services are always repaired faster
Callers wait and run out of capacity
Slow services write bigger log files
steps.why: Waiting requests pile up and starve healthy ones.

steps.q: What does an open breaker do?
choices: Retries each call harder and faster
Deletes the service and starts again
Sends the same call to every server
Fails calls fast, shows a fallback
steps.why: It gives the failing service room to recover.

steps.q: A timeout of 30 seconds on a 100 ms service is:
choices: Fine, since waiting longer is safer
Far too long for a 100 ms service
Required by most databases
Too short to ever work
steps.why: You would wait 300 times longer than normal before giving up.

takeaway: Wait briefly, stop calling what is failing, and have a fallback.

title: Surviving a region
summary: A whole region can go dark. Run in two, and send people to the one that is up.

steps.title: Zones and regions
steps.text: A zone is one data centre building; a region is a city-sized group of zones. Spreading over zones survives a fire in one building. A whole region can still fail, which is rare (a few hours a year at most, approx.) but real. Surviving it means a second region with its own copy of the data.

steps.prompt: The whole home region will go down at noon. Keep a second region ready and send traffic to it.
steps.hint: Add servers set to Europe, connect the global balancer to them, add a Read replica in Europe fed by the database, and connect the European servers to it.

steps.title: The price
steps.text: A second region costs about double and brings new problems: copies are far apart, so writes to two places can disagree. Many teams keep one writing region and a standby, or give each user a home region.

rows.label: Cost of a second full region
Moving traffic away from a dead region

steps.q: Zones protect against:
choices: A bad release reaching users
One data centre building failing
A whole region going dark
A slow query on the database
steps.why: Zones are separate buildings inside one region.

steps.q: What must a second region have to be useful?
choices: A different colour scheme
Fewer servers than the first region
Its own separate brand name
A matching set of the data it serves
steps.why: Servers without data cannot answer.

steps.q: Why is writing in two regions hard?
choices: Regions cannot send messages to each other
Two places can change one item differently
It is against the rules in most countries
The data is far too large to move
steps.why: The changes must be reconciled, and that is where conflicts arise.

takeaway: Multiple regions buy survival at the price of cost and harder data.

title: Seeing problems early
summary: You cannot fix what you cannot see: metrics, alerts and a way back.

steps.title: Three questions
steps.text: When something breaks you need: is it broken (metrics and alerts), where (logs and traces), and how do I undo it (a safe rollback). Without them, problems are found by angry users, 30 minutes later (approx.).

steps.prompt: A bad release will go out at noon. Set up watching and a quick way back.
steps.hint: Place Metrics, Alerting, Pager and CI/CD, and connect each one to the servers.

steps.title: Alerts that matter
steps.text: Alert on what people feel (errors, slow pages), not on every graph. Too many alerts and nobody reads them. A page to a human should mean something needs a human now.

steps.q: What does an alert tell you?
choices: Exactly how to fix it
The root cause of the problem
Something is wrong right now
Which team to blame
steps.why: It starts the response; logs and traces help find the cause.

steps.q: What speeds up the fix of a bad release most?
choices: Adding more servers to the busy tier
Doubling the size of the cache
Waiting to see if it clears up
A fast rollback to the last good one
steps.why: Undoing the change returns you to a working state.

steps.q: Why not alert on every metric?
choices: It costs too much to send alerts
Metrics are unable to raise alerts
People start ignoring all of them
The alerts arrive far too slowly
steps.why: Noise hides the real problem.

takeaway: Watch what users feel, tell a human fast, and keep a way back.

title: Where the money goes
summary: Every box has a monthly price. Good design meets the goal without waste.

steps.title: Idle is expensive
steps.text: Servers cost money whether they are busy or not. The usual waste is running peak capacity all day, keeping data on expensive storage, and sending data across regions and the internet. A good design is not the biggest; it is the cheapest one that still meets the goals.

steps.prompt: This system costs far too much for its traffic. Bring the monthly cost under budget without breaking it.
steps.hint: Select the servers and turn on Autoscale with a low minimum, instead of running 40 all day.

rows.label: Sending data out to the internet

steps.q: What is the cheapest way to cope with a short daily peak?
choices: Run peak-sized servers all day long
Buy the single biggest server there is
Switch the database off at night
Add servers only while the peak lasts
steps.why: You pay for extra capacity only when it is used.

steps.q: Which cost grows with every request?
choices: A yearly software licence
Data sent out with each request
A reserved server you rent monthly
Storing yesterday's backup
steps.why: Per-gigabyte transfer prices add up with traffic.

steps.q: The best design is:
choices: The most reliable one at any cost
The newest one on the market
The cheapest that meets the goals
The one with the most parts
steps.why: Goals first, then cost.

takeaway: Meet the goal with the least you can; money is a requirement too.

title: Proof built in
summary: Auditors want proof: who did what, who can see what, and that data is protected.

steps.title: Prove it, do not promise it
steps.text: Handling health, money or personal data comes with rules. An audit asks for evidence, not promises: a log nobody can edit, encryption with managed keys, one controlled place for personal data, tested backups, and a sign-in for every action.

steps.prompt: An audit lands at noon. Add what the auditors will ask for.
steps.hint: Place Audit log, Key management, Identity provider and Backups, then connect them to the servers and the database.

steps.title: Least privilege
steps.text: Give each person and each service only the access it needs, and record every use of it. Keep secrets out of code, and rotate keys. Most breaches come from a leaked key or an over-powered account, not from clever hacking.

rows.label: Test a backup restore
rows.how: an untested backup is a hope, approx.

steps.q: What does an auditor ask for?
choices: Promises that you will do better soon
A discount on the next audit
A tour of the whole office
Evidence you did what you said
steps.why: Logs, settings and test results.

steps.q: Where do secrets belong?
choices: Inside the source code itself
In a managed secrets vault
In a pinned team chat message
In a shared team spreadsheet
steps.why: Code gets copied and leaked.

steps.q: What is least privilege?
choices: Every team member gets admin rights
Access is shared by the whole team
Nobody can ever log in at all
Only the access a job needs
steps.why: Fewer powers mean smaller mistakes.

takeaway: Build the proof in from the start; adding it after the audit is far harder.

title: GPUs, tokens and fallbacks
summary: Serving AI answers is slow and expensive, so cache, limit, and have a fallback.

steps.title: Costly answers
steps.text: A chatbot answer needs a GPU, a chip that costs a few dollars an hour to rent (approx.) and can serve only a few conversations at once. Answers are measured in tokens, roughly three quarters of a word. Longer answers take longer and cost more, and the number of GPUs you can get is limited.

steps.prompt: A GPU shortage hits at noon. Add a fallback and remember repeated questions.
steps.hint: Place a Semantic cache in front of the model and a Hosted model API as a backup, with an LLM gateway to choose between them.

steps.title: Smaller and cached
steps.text: Many questions are the same or similar, so a semantic cache can answer from memory. A smaller model handles easy questions and a bigger one the hard ones. Limits on answer length keep cost predictable.

steps.q: Why is AI serving expensive?
choices: Every answer is stored for years in a vault
A person has to read each answer first
Each answer keeps a costly GPU busy
The model is retrained for each user
steps.why: Each answer ties up a chip for seconds.

steps.q: A semantic cache helps when:
choices: Every single question is completely new
Many people ask nearly the same thing
The answers must differ every time
Nobody uses the system at all
steps.why: Similar questions can share one answer.

steps.q: What is a good plan for a GPU shortage?
choices: Wait until the shortage passes by itself
Delete the busiest GPUs to save power
Turn off the load balancer for a while
Fall back to a hosted or smaller model
steps.why: Serve degraded answers rather than none.

takeaway: Cache, cap and fall back; GPUs are the scarcest part of the system.

title: Consistent hashing and moving data
summary: Adding one machine can mean moving a little data or nearly all of it.

steps.title: One new machine, a long night
steps.text: You have eight storage nodes and 8 TB of user records. You add a ninth. The disks have room, but the next morning is spent copying records while live requests wait. Placement decides how much work a small expansion causes. Hashing a user id spreads keys. It does not by itself tell you how to change the number of owners safely.

steps.title: Keep most owners in place
steps.text: With hash(key) mod N, changing N changes nearly every remainder. For uniform hashes and a move from 8 to 9, only about 1/9 of keys keep the same numbered owner. About 8/9 move. On a ring, hash both keys and node positions into the same space. A key belongs to the next node clockwise. A new ring position takes part of its clockwise successor's range. With virtual nodes, one physical machine takes ranges from several owners. In a balanced 8 to 9 expansion, about 1/9 of logical data changes owner. Virtual nodes put many positions per machine on the ring. They smooth random imbalance and let larger machines take more ranges. They do not make one hot key smaller.

steps.title: Worked example: moving 8 TB
steps.text: Assume uniformly hashed data of roughly equal record size, no replicas and decimal TB. Modulo placement moves about 7.11 TB; a balanced ring moves about 0.89 TB. At a reserved 100 MB/s, the ring copy alone takes about 8,900 seconds, or 2.5 hours. Modulo needs about 19.8 hours. These are lower bounds: reads, checksums, retries and catching up new writes also use disk and network. Replication changes the bytes and failure headroom. This is a worked example because the sim does not model range movement.

rows.label: Copy floor
rows.how: 0.89 TB ÷ 100 MB/s; excludes catch-up and replicas

steps.q: Eight equal nodes hold 8 TB without replicas. A balanced ring adds a ninth. Which plan preserves live writes during the move?
choices: Copy about 0.89 TB and switch after snapshot checksums match
Copy about 0.89 TB, replay changes, then fence the old owner at cutover
Copy about 7.11 TB while retaining the ring placement
steps.why: A snapshot can miss writes made during copying. Catch-up and a fenced ownership switch protect them.

steps.q: Why bother with a ring at only eight nodes? Follow-up: how would you prove the expansion is safe?
checklist: Compare 7.11 TB of modulo movement with 0.89 TB on a balanced ring
Reserve copy bandwidth alongside foreground and replica work
Fence stale owners and verify snapshot checksums plus replay offsets
steps.model: I would first ask how often capacity changes. A stable small database may need no custom ring at all. For frequent changes, reducing a 7.11 TB copy to about 0.89 TB matters. I would reserve migration bandwidth, watch p99 and replica lag, copy and catch up each range, then fence the old owner and switch a versioned map. Stale routers must forward or retry rather than creating another writable copy. Counts and checksums plus write-log offsets establish that the new owner is ready. Old owners stay until verification and a bounded rollback window finish.

steps.title: Move ownership as carefully as bytes
steps.text: Publish a versioned placement map. Copy a snapshot of a range, replay changes made during the copy, then fence the old writer and switch routing with an explicit ownership version. Reject or forward writes carrying stale ownership; a new map alone does not stop them. Keep a forwarding or retry path while clients learn the new map. Delete the old copy only after checking the new owner and the rollback window. Rate limit copying against foreground p99, not just available bandwidth. A hot tenant may need subkeys, a cache for repeated reads, or a dedicated placement. More virtual nodes cannot split a single record's writes.

steps.q: One partition key receives 40% of writes. What does doubling virtual nodes do to that key?
choices: It divides that key across twice as many replica sets
It lets replicas independently accept half its writes without reconciliation
It keeps one replica set; other ranges may balance better
steps.why: Virtual nodes divide hash ranges, not one key. Splitting writes needs a different key or protocol.

steps.q: We added nodes and p99 got worse. What would you inspect? Follow-up: the hottest key still overloads one owner.
checklist: Inspect migration I/O, cold caches and stale-map retries
Compare bytes per range with write rate on the hottest key
Explain how subkeys change reads or ordering before splitting writes
steps.model: I would separate migration I/O from user I/O and check cold caches, range skew and routing retries. Equal bytes do not imply equal work. If repeated reads dominate, caching may help. If one key takes too many writes, use a deliberate subkey scheme with aggregation or a dedicated owner. That changes reads or ordering, so I would test the business invariant before splitting it.

steps.q: The snapshot and change replay are complete, but routers still use two map versions. What protects subsequent writes?
choices: Fence old ownership and forward or retry stale-routed requests
Keep both owners writable until every router reports the new map
Delete the old copy as soon as snapshot checksums match
steps.why: Catch-up proves a past state. Fencing stops old routers creating a second write authority after cutover.

takeaway: Plan the ownership change and the bytes it moves, not just the final node count.

title: Copies and quorums
summary: Copies tolerate failures when placement, acknowledgements and repair match the promise.

steps.title: The copy that missed a write
steps.text: Three replicas hold a delivery address. One is offline when the address changes. The next read reaches that copy first. More copies improved durability, but the answer is old. A replication factor names how many copies should exist. A read or write quorum names how many replies an operation must wait for.

steps.title: What overlap proves
steps.text: Let N be the number of replicas in a fixed set, W the durable write acknowledgements and R the read replies. If R + W > N, every read set overlaps every completed write set. For N = 3 and R = W = 2, a read started after a completed write contacts at least one replica that accepted it. That replica may now hold a superseding version. The coordinator or client must compare versions and reconcile replies. Intersection alone does not make concurrent writes linearizable. Failed partial writes, sloppy quorums that use substitute nodes, clock-based conflict resolution and membership changes need extra rules. A quorum is a building block, not a transaction.

steps.title: Worked example: a zone goes dark
steps.text: Put one replica in each of three zones. R = 2 and W = 2 can continue with one replica down, if both remaining replicas answer. W = 3 cannot complete then. Suppose local durable work is 2 ms and reaching the fastest remote replica adds a 3 ms round trip. A write waiting for local plus remote has a rough floor of 5 ms. If it needs an 80 ms cross-region trip instead, expect about 82 ms before queueing. Fan-out can be parallel; do not sum every replica trip. The sim cannot reproduce individual replica acknowledgements, so these are protocol calculations.

rows.label: Zone write floor
rows.how: 2 ms durable work + 3 ms remote RTT, illustrative

rows.label: Physical payload
rows.how: 10 TB logical × replication factor 3, before indexes

steps.q: With fixed N = 3, R = 1 and W = 2, one replica missed a completed write. What does the next read guarantee?
choices: It sees the write because W is a majority
It may return the old value if it chooses that replica
It sees the write if hinted handoff is enabled
steps.why: R + W equals N, so the read and write sets can be disjoint. Hints may repair the stale replica later.

steps.q: R plus W is bigger than N. Why will you not promise linearizability yet? Follow-up: two writers race.
checklist: State fixed membership and reconcile versions from intersecting sets
Explain racing writers and reads that expose partial writes
Name the read and write rules needed for a linearizable register
steps.model: Intersection only guarantees contact with a replica from each completed write set. Racing writers still need unique ordered versions, and a partial write can be seen by one read then missed by another. For a linearizable quorum register, I would choose a proven protocol: writers obtain a tag above those observed in a quorum, then durably write it to a quorum; readers select the highest tag and write it back to a quorum before returning. Tags include a writer identity to break ties. A leader with consensus and safe reads is another option. The read and recovery rules, not R and W alone, establish the guarantee.

steps.title: Repair is scheduled work
steps.text: Read repair compares returned versions and updates stale replicas on the read path. Hinted handoff stores a reminder of a missed write and replays it when the missing owner returns. Hints have bounded lifetime and consume disk; they do not replace anti-entropy repair of all ranges. A quiet record may never be read. Repair within the deletion-retention window. In Cassandra, a replica that missed a deletion can resurrect data after the tombstone is purged. If the outage exceeds that window, rebuild the stale replica from current data rather than trusting ordinary repair alone. Otherwise compare and repair all affected ranges before declaring it current. Keep repair bandwidth below the level that breaks foreground requests. Count physical copies in the storage bill, and place them across failure domains rather than three processes on one host.

steps.q: Fixed N = 5, R = 3, W = 3. Two replicas are unreachable. Which operations can still meet these counts?
choices: Reads and writes, if all three survivors reply
Reads only; durable writes need four survivors
Writes only; a read must also contact a failed replica
steps.why: Three survivors satisfy both thresholds. Membership, durability and version reconciliation still need a protocol.

steps.q: Can we lower cross-zone write latency by acknowledging only the local copy? Follow-up: that zone disappears.
checklist: Explain which acknowledged writes survive loss of the local zone
Calculate the illustrative local and remote waits
Describe the unavailable-zone policy and repair headroom
steps.model: Acknowledging locally removes a network wait but changes the failure promise. The newest acknowledged writes may exist only in that zone. If the requirement is to survive its loss without losing acknowledged data, I must wait for a durable copy outside it. I can batch or choose nearby zones, but I cannot remove the communication requirement. Hints help restore a missing replica later; they cannot recover the only copy after it is destroyed. With 2 ms durable work and a 3 ms required remote round trip, the illustrative floor is 5 ms; an 80 ms trip makes it 82 ms. If the remote acknowledgement is unavailable, I must defer writes or explicitly weaken durability. Repair needs reserved bandwidth so recovery does not overload the survivors.

steps.q: A replica missed writes after its hints expired. Tombstones still cover the outage. What establishes that cold keys are current?
choices: Run quorum reads for the busiest keys until latency settles
Wait for its normal heartbeat and successful health checks
Repair all affected ranges and verify completion
steps.why: Popular-key reads leave cold ranges unchecked. A healthy process is not evidence of current data.

takeaway: Name the replica set, acknowledgement count, failure model and reconciliation rule together.

title: Agreeing on one leader
summary: A leader needs a safe election and a way to stop old owners from acting.

steps.title: Two schedulers both think they own the job
steps.text: A scheduler pauses for twenty seconds. Its lease expires, so another scheduler takes over. The first wakes and sends an invoice anyway. A lease can tell the service who should own a job. It cannot stop a paused process from using an old decision. Choosing one leader and enforcing that choice are separate parts of the design.

steps.title: Raft in plain words
steps.text: Raft keeps a replicated sequence of decisions. A follower whose randomized election timeout expires without valid leader contact becomes a candidate in a new term and asks for votes. Each voter persists at most one vote per term and only votes for a candidate whose log is sufficiently up to date. A majority elects a leader. The leader appends entries and replicates them; it can advance commit by counting a majority for an entry from its current term, which also commits the preceding log. Servers apply committed decisions in order. A linearizable read also needs a current-term committed entry, confirmation of current authority, and application through the read index; a stale leader cannot safely answer from memory alone. Elections alone are not consensus: log rules preserve decisions through later elections. This assumes crash faults, not malicious voters.

steps.title: Worked example: a five-node split
steps.text: Five voters need three. In a 3 versus 2 partition, the three can elect and commit; the two cannot. With a 2 versus 2 versus 1 split, nobody can commit. Two majorities always share a voter, but persistent voting and log rules are what make that intersection useful. An isolated old leader can still believe it is leader in an older term. It must not serve unsafe reads or issue unfenced effects. The game does not model Raft terms or logs, so this example is arithmetic, not a live election.

rows.label: Three voters
rows.how: Tolerates one unavailable voter; often enough

rows.label: Fencing boundary
rows.how: Durably compare tokens where the side effect is accepted

steps.q: Five fixed Raft voters split into groups of three and two. What can the two-node side promise without contacting the other side?
choices: Latest reads from its previously elected leader, while pausing writes
New commits after both surviving voters agree on a higher term
Only explicitly stale reads; majority operations must wait or fail
steps.why: Two voters cannot form a majority of five. An old leader cannot infer current authority from local state.

steps.q: We have a majority election. How could we still send an invoice twice? Follow-up: the provider does not accept fencing tokens.
checklist: Show how a paused old leader can still call the invoice provider
Persist one operation and reuse its provider key across leaders
State what remains ambiguous without provider deduplication
steps.model: A paused old leader can still send a delayed provider call after a new leader takes over. I would fence our local state and persist one invoice intent with an outbox. Every leader and retry reuses the same provider idempotency key. A status lookup helps reconcile, but a negative result alone cannot rule out a request still in flight. Without provider deduplication or another atomic acceptance rule, election alone cannot guarantee exactly one external effect. I would document the duplicate-versus-missing risk and the manual reconciliation path.

steps.title: Make stale ownership harmless
steps.text: Give each ownership grant a durable increasing fencing token. The resource that accepts a write atomically compares the token, records the highest accepted token and performs the write, rejecting older tokens. If owner 41 pauses and owner 42 writes, a later request carrying 41 is rejected by the resource. A check in the old process is insufficient. A coordination service is useful for small shared decisions: membership, leases and ownership maps. It is a poor place for every user record or high-volume event. If a database transaction, a unique constraint or a managed queue already owns the invariant, use that instead. Keep the coordination cluster independent enough to survive the failures it must resolve.

steps.q: A worker checks its lease, then pauses. A new owner writes before it resumes. What rejects the delayed old write?
choices: An atomic token comparison and write at the storage resource
Renewing the lease immediately before sending the write
Checking the current token in a separate storage request before writing
steps.why: A separate check leaves another pause window. The receiver must enforce fencing atomically with the effect.

steps.q: Should every request consult the coordination service? Follow-up: its quorum is down for ten minutes.
checklist: Use the coordinator for ownership changes rather than every user request
Specify when cached authority expires and where fencing is enforced
Stop exclusive operations when valid authority cannot be renewed
steps.model: I would cache a versioned owner map and use the coordinator for changes. Existing owners can work only within the protocol's valid authority, with receiver-side fencing. If fresh authority cannot be obtained, operations that require exclusive ownership stop. Public cached reads may continue under a separate promise. Losing a quorum should not silently create two owners. I would consider whether an existing transactional store could own this small decision more simply.

steps.q: SQL already enforces exclusive invoice ownership. Which requirement could justify an additional coordination service?
choices: Electing a worker so provider calls no longer need idempotency
Coordinating ownership of resources outside that database transaction
Caching the SQL owner row so expired ownership is always safe to reuse
steps.why: A separate invariant may need coordination. Election does not deduplicate external effects or make cached authority permanent.

takeaway: Consensus preserves one committed order; fencing carries that authority to the resource.

title: What consistent really means
summary: Choose the guarantee for each operation and name what a partition changes.

steps.title: The balance and the activity list disagree
steps.text: A transfer succeeds. The balance screen shows the debit, but a refreshed activity list does not. Later, a refresh shows an even older list. These are different failures. A product can need a current balance, read-your-writes on confirmation, and monotonic reads while paging history without demanding the same guarantee everywhere.

steps.title: Separate time from transactions
steps.text: Linearizability makes each operation appear to take effect at one instant between its call and reply, respecting real-time order. Serializability makes concurrent transactions equivalent to some serial order. That order need not respect wall-clock order; strict serializability adds that requirement. Snapshot isolation lets a transaction read a stable committed snapshot and prevents concurrent transactions that write the same item from both committing. It can still allow write skew across different items. Read-your-writes prevents your later reads missing your own successful writes. Monotonic reads prevent a session moving backwards through versions. Neither session guarantee alone makes every reader see the latest value.

steps.title: Worked example: nobody is on call
steps.text: Two doctors are on call. Each transaction reads a snapshot with both doctors present, checks that another doctor remains, and turns its own row off. They write different rows, so snapshot isolation can let both commit. The result has zero doctors. Serializable execution would reject at least one transaction or force it to see the first change. A shared roster guard can work if every writer locks it before checking current roster state; acquiring it after a stale snapshot check is insufficient. An atomic conditional update on one roster record can also enforce the invariant. This is a transaction schedule, not a demo: the sim cannot execute concurrent SQL transactions.

rows.label: Write skew outcome
rows.how: Two snapshots see 2; each removes a different doctor

rows.label: Remote coordination floor
rows.how: 10 ms local path + 80 ms required RTT

rows.label: Session catch-up
rows.how: 300 writes/s × 2 s lag; a version token can require waiting

steps.q: A balance transaction is serializable. What does that alone establish about a later read from an asynchronous replica?
choices: It must include the transaction because the write was serializable
Its freshness still needs a read-routing or version guarantee
It is current once the replica reports that it is healthy
steps.why: Serializability orders transactions. It does not by itself make an asynchronous replica current.

steps.q: Why is saying our database is strongly consistent insufficient? Follow-up: choose guarantees for a reservation, save confirmation and public count.
checklist: Choose an atomic reservation, read-your-writes confirmation and stale public count
Explain overselling, a missing saved edit and tolerable stale counts
State which operations wait during a partition
steps.model: I need to know which operations, which replicas and which failure conditions that phrase covers. A last-seat reservation needs an atomic invariant, often a serializable transaction or conditional write. A save confirmation needs read-your-writes, perhaps by routing to an authority or waiting for a version. A public count can accept bounded staleness. During a partition I would defer the reservation, keep a local pending edit visible and label stale public data. The latency and availability costs differ by screen.

steps.title: Partitions and ordinary days
steps.text: CAP says that during a network partition you cannot guarantee both linearizable behavior and a successful response to every request at every nonfailed node. Its availability definition is stricter than an uptime percentage. It does not say pick two features forever, and partition tolerance is not a convenient switch in a real network. PACELC extends this: during partitions, consider availability versus consistency; otherwise ask what latency you pay for coordination to get the chosen consistency. Suppose an app and local store take 10 ms while a remote round trip takes 80 ms. A protocol requiring that remote reply has a rough floor near 90 ms. Choose per screen: session versions or primary reads for confirmation, a serializable reservation for the last seat, and bounded staleness for a public count. State how each screen behaves while separated.

steps.q: Both doctors leave under snapshot isolation after reading the other as on call. Which remedy protects the roster invariant?
choices: Add optimistic version checks only to each doctor's own row
Lock each doctor's own row after reading both rows
Use serializable transactions with retries or a shared guard locked before checking
steps.why: The transactions update different rows. Own-row checks and locks do not serialize the shared roster check.

steps.q: Why not make every read linearizable? Follow-up: we have users an ocean away.
checklist: Calculate the illustrative 10 ms local path plus 80 ms remote trip
Choose a freshness bound for cached public summaries
Keep allocation decisions at a safe authority despite remote latency
steps.model: With the example's 10 ms local path and 80 ms remote trip, a required remote reply gives a rough 90 ms floor before queueing. Some protocols can serve safe local reads, but only under explicit lease, quorum or leadership rules. I would spend that coordination on decisions such as allocating money or stock, and avoid it for public summaries. The test is whether a stale result can cause harm and what the next action validates. A faster stale summary still needs a clear freshness promise.

steps.q: A partition isolates a region from the only seat-allocation authority. There are no preallocated regional rights. Which policy avoids overselling?
choices: Serve marked stale counts but defer exclusive seat claims
Accept local claims and reconcile duplicate seats after recovery
Accept claims while a cached count still shows available seats
steps.why: A stale count cannot allocate exclusive seats safely. Offline allocation would require a separate rights protocol.

takeaway: Ask which operation, which order and which failure, then choose the smallest sufficient guarantee.

title: Inside a storage engine
summary: The path from a write to disk decides memory, I/O and cost.

steps.title: Fast inserts, then a sudden stall
steps.text: An import runs well for ten minutes, then write latency climbs even though incoming traffic is flat. The database is merging files in the background. An acknowledged byte can be written several times over its life. Capacity planning that counts only the incoming payload misses that work.

steps.title: Two ways to keep keys sorted
steps.text: For a durable WAL-backed commit, persist the log through the promised failure boundary before acknowledging. Appending to a process buffer alone is insufficient. Recovery replays committed log records and ignores or undoes incomplete work as the engine requires. A B-tree stores sorted keys in pages, updating affected pages and sometimes splitting them. A buffer pool turns many random I/Os into memory access, but dirty pages still reach disk. An LSM tree first appends to a log and updates a sorted in-memory memtable. It later flushes the memtable into immutable sorted files called SSTables. Compaction merges files, drops obsolete versions when safe and rewrites surviving keys. B-trees also use logs and background work. Neither name alone predicts the winner; measure the access pattern and working set.

steps.title: Worked example: the hidden writes
steps.text: Suppose logical ingestion is 20 MB/s. Assume measured total device write amplification is 10, including WAL, flushes and compaction in this workload. The device must sustain about 200 MB/s, or 17.28 TB written per day. With three replicas that becomes about 51.84 TB/day across devices, before unrelated work. If each device can safely sustain 300 MB/s for this workload, it has limited space for repair and bursts. These are explicit assumptions, not universal LSM ratios. The sim models store capacities but not SSTables or disk endurance.

steps.q: Logical writes are 20 MB/s and measured total device write amplification is 10. What device bandwidth is needed before headroom?
choices: About 20 MB/s because compaction runs in the background
About 200 MB/s
About 60 MB/s after allowing one WAL write and one flush
steps.why: The measured total already includes WAL, flushes and compaction: 20 × 10 = 200 MB/s.

steps.q: The SSD vendor quotes 1 GB/s. Why will you not promise 1 GB/s of user writes? Follow-up: include replication.
checklist: Divide 1 GB/s device bandwidth by amplification ten before headroom
Count three replicas across the fleet without charging each device three times
Benchmark p99 with durable commits, reads, compaction and repair
steps.model: That figure may be sequential bandwidth under a different workload. If total amplification is ten, 1 GB/s of device writes supports at most 100 MB/s logical writes before headroom. Three full replicas triple fleet device work, not necessarily each device's incoming share. I would benchmark durable acknowledgements with compaction, reads and repair active. I would also check endurance, temporary disk space and tail latency before quoting a safe ingest rate.

steps.title: Reads pay too
steps.text: An LSM lookup may check memory and several candidate files. A Bloom filter can say definitely absent or maybe present for a key in a file. A positive result still requires a lookup; a false positive wastes I/O. Filters do not return the value, and a range scan still needs data. At roughly 10 bits per key, a well-tuned Bloom filter has about a 1% false-positive rate. For 100 million keys that is about 125 MB before overhead. More filter and cache memory can reduce reads. Compaction style trades write amplification, read amplification and temporary disk space. Choose hardware from measured p99, IOPS, sequential bandwidth, memory and endurance, with repair and compaction running together.

steps.q: A file's Bloom filter says a key may be present. What does a correct point lookup do next?
choices: Return absent unless a second Bloom filter agrees
Treat the positive as proof and skip checking the key in the data
Check the candidate data through the cache or file index
steps.why: A positive can be false. A filter identifies candidate files but cannot return or confirm a value.

steps.q: Can we stop compaction to make today's writes faster? Follow-up: what happens tomorrow?
checklist: Explain how paused compaction increases files, reads and disk use
Pair temporary throttling with an admission limit and deadline
Monitor pending compaction bytes and reserve catch-up bandwidth
steps.model: Pausing compaction can temporarily free I/O, but files and obsolete versions accumulate. Reads may check more files, disk fills and later compaction needs extra bandwidth. I might reduce its rate briefly during an incident while also reducing admitted writes. I would set a deadline, watch pending compaction bytes and disk space, and reserve a measured catch-up window. It is borrowing capacity, not creating it.

steps.q: A new workload fits in RAM, but must survive crashes. Which evidence best supports choosing B-tree or LSM storage?
choices: Steady-state benchmarks with durability, reads and background work enabled
A ten-minute insert benchmark that ends before compaction starts
A cache-hit benchmark with WAL synchronization disabled
steps.why: The working set may fit in RAM while durable writes and background I/O still control sustained performance.

takeaway: Size the physical reads, writes and memory under background work, not just the incoming payload.

title: Work across services
summary: Make each step durable and show the user what is still pending.

steps.title: Charged, but no order
steps.text: Checkout calls inventory, then payments, then delivery. The payment succeeds just as the order service crashes. A retry cannot tell whether to charge again. There is no single database transaction across these services. The business needs a durable story for each intermediate state, including an unknown result.

steps.title: Choose the transaction boundary
steps.text: Two-phase commit asks participants to prepare, then asks them to commit once the coordinator decides. Prepared resources can hold locks while a failed coordinator or network delays the decision. It is useful in some managed transactional systems, but uncommon across independently operated services and external APIs that do not support it. A saga commits local steps and uses explicit compensating actions when later steps fail. Compensation is a new business action, such as a refund, not time travel. Fees, messages already seen and shipments already sent cannot always be undone.

steps.title: Worked example: one durable order
steps.text: In one local transaction, save order 730 as pending and an outbox row with event id 730:created. A relay publishes it, then crashes before marking it sent. It publishes again after restart. Inventory records the event id and the reservation in one local transaction, so a repeat returns the saved result. Payments use one stable payment key and store pending, succeeded or failed. A timeout means unknown, so reconcile with the provider. If payment later succeeds after stock was released, refund it and explain that state to the customer. This worked schedule exposes crash boundaries that the sim does not execute.

steps.q: An outbox relay publishes, then crashes before marking the row sent. What protects a consumer's local effect on replay?
choices: Producer-side broker deduplication alone
A consumer cache of seen ids updated before the database mutation
A unique event id committed with the effect and saved result
steps.why: A relay can republish, and a consumer can crash too. The deduplication record and local effect must commit together.

steps.q: Why not use two-phase commit for checkout? Follow-up: are sagas equally atomic?
checklist: Check provider participation and locks held by prepared transactions
Name pending payment and refund states visible during a saga
Explain why a refund cannot undo fees or a shipment already sent
steps.model: Our payment provider does not participate in our transaction, and holding inventory locks across a network failure is expensive. A saga fits local ownership, but it is not equally atomic: people may see an order waiting or a refund pending. I would define those states with product and finance, use stable keys, and reconcile unknown outcomes. If a closed set of databases provides a supported distributed transaction with acceptable availability, two-phase commit may still be a reasonable choice.

steps.title: Bound the unfinished work
steps.text: A broker acknowledgement is not proof that an order shipped. Persist saga state, retry with jitter, and alert on the age of pending work. Consumers need their own deduplication and local atomicity. Give each compensation its own stable key too. At 200 orders/s and a 30-minute downstream outage, about 360,000 orders accumulate. At 2 KB of durable workflow state each, that is about 720 MB before indexes and replicas. If recovery handles 500/s while new arrivals remain 200/s, net drain is 300/s and catch-up takes about 20 minutes. The UI should show received, awaiting payment, confirmed, refund pending and refunded as appropriate. Set a deadline and a support path for states automation cannot settle.

steps.q: Checkout times out while calling a provider that may have accepted the charge. What should it do?
choices: Show pending and reconcile using the same payment key
Mark failed and submit a new key so the customer can retry
Release the order and treat a later provider success as unrelated
steps.why: A timeout leaves an unknown outcome. Preserve the logical payment identity and handle a late success explicitly.

steps.q: Where exactly is the idempotency key stored? Follow-up: the worker crashes between checking the key and applying the change.
checklist: Enforce event-key uniqueness in the inventory authority
Commit deduplication, stock mutation and saved result together
Persist external intent and reconcile with the same provider key
steps.model: A separate cache check leaves a race. For a local inventory change I insert the unique event key, reserve stock and save the result in one transaction. A duplicate returns that result. For external effects I reuse the same provider idempotency key and use status lookup to reconcile. A negative lookup alone does not rule out an original request still in flight, so it cannot make blind resubmission safe. I persist an intent before the call and reconcile its outcome after a crash. No local table alone makes an unsupported external call exactly once.

steps.q: Workers handle 250/s while arrivals stay at 300/s. No work expires or is shed. What happens to the backlog?
choices: It drains at 250/s because all workers are running
It grows by 50/s until service or admissions change
It stops growing once retries use stable operation ids
steps.why: Deduplication avoids repeated effects, but unique arrivals still exceed service by 50/s.

takeaway: Commit locally, publish through an outbox, and make every later effect safe to repeat or reconcile.

title: Ordering and time
summary: A timestamp can sort events without proving which event caused another.

steps.title: The older edit wins
steps.text: A laptop clock is five minutes fast. It edits a title, then a phone edits the same title after receiving that change. A last-write-wins rule using device time can keep the laptop's older title. The timestamps look precise, but they do not prove the order people acted in.
