Clock sync reduces error; it does not remove uncertainty or pauses.

steps.title: Order only what you know
steps.text: A Lamport clock is a counter. Increment it for local events; on receipt, set it above both the local and received counter. If A caused B, A has a smaller timestamp. The reverse is not true: smaller numbers do not prove causality. Adding a node id breaks ties into a total order, but invents an order for concurrent work. A vector clock keeps one counter per participant. Comparing vectors can show that one history includes another, or that neither includes the other and the edits are concurrent. Participant identity, pruning and metadata growth are real design costs.

steps.title: Worked example: concurrent edits
steps.text: Two devices start with vector [0,0]. Offline, laptop writes title A at [1,0]; phone writes title B at [0,1]. Neither vector dominates, so there is a conflict. After seeing both, a resolving edit on the laptop can carry [2,1]. It includes both histories. Last-write-wins would silently discard one title unless a conflict copy is kept. A CRDT instead defines merge rules whose operations or states converge under stated delivery and causality assumptions. A grow-only counter can merge each device's component by maximum. Values [4,0] and [0,3] merge to [4,3], total 7. Do not sum repeated snapshots. The sim does not model these histories, so this is a worked example.

rows.label: Clock error
rows.how: A five-minute fast device can beat later wall-clock writes

steps.q: Lamport(A) is smaller than Lamport(B). What can the counters alone establish?
choices: A is an ancestor in B's causal history
A occurred earlier in wall-clock time within clock-sync error
They do not distinguish causal order from concurrency
steps.why: Causality implies increasing Lamport time. Increasing Lamport time does not imply causality or wall-clock order.

steps.q: Why not use last-write-wins for notes? Follow-up: users rarely edit at the same time.
checklist: Show how a fast device clock can discard a causally later edit
Compare the harm of losing a note with the measured conflict rate
Preserve conflict versions or define a tested field or text merge
steps.model: It may be acceptable for a low-value preference with a clear timestamp rule. A note can hold irreplaceable work. Rare conflicts still hurt, and device clocks can make a causally later edit lose. I would retain conflicting versions or use a field or text merge suited to the editor, with a visible recovery path. I would measure conflicts before adopting a complex CRDT, but never equate a low conflict rate with permission to silently delete work.

steps.title: Convergence is not every invariant
steps.text: Sets need rules for concurrent add and remove. Text needs stable operation identities and a deliberate policy for concurrent inserts and deletes. CRDTs do not automatically protect a global stock limit or make a merged document useful to its author. A bounded inventory decrement may require coordination or preallocated rights. Order matters for debits against a balance, seat allocation and commands with dependencies. It often need not be global for independent counters or separate users' edits. Prefer per-key order, preserve causal dependencies and retain enough history to explain a conflict. If the requirement says newest, ask newest by whose observation.

steps.q: Vectors [3,1] and [2,2] describe edits to one field. How should a causal merge classify them?
choices: Concurrent; neither vector includes the other history
The first is later because its largest component is larger
They describe the same version because both components sum to four
steps.why: Each vector is larger in one component. Summing counters discards the participant information needed to compare histories.

steps.q: Do we need one global event order? Follow-up: payments and click counters share the stream.
checklist: Separate account spending decisions from independent click counts
Scope authority and stream order to the account or other invariant key
Preserve event ids and causal links when workflows cross partitions
steps.model: A payment account needs an authority for spending decisions, while independent click counters can merge. A single global order would couple unrelated tenants and limit throughput. I would partition by the invariant's key, retain stable event ids and causal references where workflows cross keys, and explicitly coordinate the few operations that require a shared decision. A stream's per-partition sequence is not a global transaction.

steps.q: Two disconnected sellers share a convergent sold-ticket counter but have no allocated rights. What prevents overselling?
choices: Merge the counters frequently enough that both sellers eventually agree
Coordinate admission or allocate bounded rights before disconnection
Check each local counter before admitting a sale, then merge by maximum
steps.why: Local checks can both spend the last seat. Convergence alone only reveals the oversold total later.

takeaway: Use clocks to express what is known, and choose an explicit policy for concurrent work.

title: Syncing across devices
summary: Offline edits need durable local intent, a cursor and a plan for old devices.

steps.title: The note returns after you delete it
steps.text: You delete a note on your phone. A laptop has been offline for a month and later uploads its old copy. Without a record of the deletion, the server may treat that copy as new. Sync is a protocol for reconciling histories, not just downloading the current rows.

steps.title: Send changes, keep intent
steps.text: Save each local edit and a device outbox entry in one durable transaction before showing it as saved on this device. Give the operation a stable id, a device sequence and a base version. Upload retries use the same id. The server commits the operation and deduplication result together, then returns its version. An upload acknowledgement must not advance the pull cursor past other changes the device has never downloaded. Pull after the last committed pull cursor, then commit the downloaded changes and that cursor together locally. Opaque cursors may include an epoch so a rebuilt log cannot be mistaken for the old one. A lost cursor can trigger a snapshot tied to a log position, followed by deltas from that position. Preserve local unsynced edits separately during this rebase.

steps.title: Worked example: a day of edits
steps.text: A notebook has 10,000 notes averaging 2 KB. A full refresh downloads about 20 MB. If 50 notes changed today, a delta costs about 100 KB before metadata, about 200 times less. A timer scheduled every minute makes up to 1,440 polling attempts a day while allowed to run. The operating system may coalesce or suspend them; timer firings are not a measurement of radio wakeups. A push can say changes are ready so the client pulls authenticated deltas. Push is a wake-up hint, not the durable delivery channel. Sleeping phones and mobile operating systems may delay it. Under-a-second propagation is a foreground connected-device target; background delivery is eventual. The sim can show network traffic, but cannot measure radio wakeups or offline convergence.

rows.label: Minute polling attempts
rows.how: 24 × 60 if allowed to run; actual wakeups depend on the OS and radio

steps.q: A client persists its pull cursor before committing downloaded changes, then crashes. What can happen?
choices: The next pull repeats the changes because the server can see the crash
The next pull skips changes that never committed locally
The server deduplicates uploads, which also repairs the missing downloads
steps.why: The server cannot infer local application. Commit pulled changes and their cursor in one local transaction.

steps.q: Why is an on-device outbox necessary? Follow-up: the user closes the app just after an edit.
checklist: Commit the note and its upload intent in one local transaction
Say when saved locally becomes durably synced to the server
Resume the same operation id after app termination or reboot
steps.model: A network call after a local edit leaves a crash window. I would save the edit and its outbox operation together before confirming local save. On restart, the outbox resumes with the same id. The screen says saved on this device until the server durably accepts it. That does not protect against losing the device itself before syncing, and the product must make that distinction clear.

steps.title: Keep deletions and expose conflicts
steps.text: A tombstone says a particular identity was deleted at a version. Keep it until the supported offline horizon and replica recovery rules make forgetting safe. If clients may be offline for 30 days, a shorter tombstone lifetime risks resurrection. Devices returning beyond the horizon must rebase from a fresh snapshot. Validate the upload epoch or reject unknown base versions even after tombstones expire, so a missing old identity is not mistaken for a new note. Concurrent whole-note edits can become conflict copies. A text CRDT may preserve more intent but adds metadata, testing and encryption constraints. Show saved locally, syncing, synced and conflict states distinctly. Bound batches, compress deltas, back off retries and use Wi-Fi or charging policies for large attachments. Measure freshness without spending the battery on empty polls.

steps.q: A sleeping phone receives delayed push notifications. What promise can the sync protocol support?
choices: Subsecond background sync once the push provider accepts the notification
Confirmed delivery once the server persists its push outbox entry
Fast foreground sync and eventual background catch-up when the app runs
steps.why: Provider acceptance and durable intent are useful boundaries, but neither proves the phone has run or pulled changes.

steps.q: Can we delete tombstones after a week to cut storage? Follow-up: a laptop returns after a month.
checklist: Compare one-week tombstones with the supported month offline
Reject expired epochs or unknown bases before applying old uploads
Preserve unsynced edits while fetching and rebasing a fresh snapshot
steps.model: Only if our supported offline window and all recovery paths fit that week, or old clients are forced through a safe rebase. A month-old laptop cannot upload its old snapshot as truth. I would fetch a fresh snapshot, preserve its unsynced operations separately, validate base versions and surface conflicts. The extra deletion metadata buys a concrete promise about which disconnected clients can return safely.

steps.q: A device returns after its cursor and deletion history expired. How can it resume without reviving deleted notes?
choices: Fetch a snapshot, preserve queued edits and validate their old bases or surface conflicts
Fetch a snapshot, then overwrite it with all queued note bodies
Set the cursor to the current log head and upload rows missing from the snapshot
steps.why: A missing row could be a deletion. Old queued work needs version validation or user resolution, not unconditional replay.

takeaway: Save intent locally, resume with stable ids and cursors, and keep enough history to merge safely.

title: Privacy by design
summary: The safest data to protect is data the service never receives.

steps.title: A wearable knows more than the dashboard needs
steps.text: A wrist device samples motion every second. The person wants a daily activity summary, not a server-side copy of every movement. Uploading all raw readings creates a sensitive archive and an ongoing deletion obligation. Start by asking which feature needs which data, who can read it and how long it must exist.

steps.title: Move the boundary deliberately
steps.text: Data minimisation means collecting the fields, precision and retention needed for a stated purpose. On-device processing can keep raw health or location data local and upload only chosen summaries. It uses device CPU and needs a reliable local store. End-to-end encryption means only authorized endpoints hold decryption keys; TLS and encryption at rest do not provide that boundary if the service holds the keys. A server without plaintext cannot offer ordinary full-text search, content moderation or account recovery from a password reset alone. Local search and explicit encrypted backup or recovery keys change the product. Timing, account ids and sizes can still leak metadata.

steps.title: Worked example: sparse uploads
steps.text: Assume one 16-byte reading each second. That is about 1.38 MB/day per device before local indexes. Thirty days require about 41.5 MB. A 2 KB daily summary is about 690 times less payload than raw readings. The summary can still reveal health information and needs consent, authorization and retention rules. These are decimal payload calculations, not a radio-energy measurement. The sim cannot prove device isolation, encryption or legal compliance; a passing traffic day does not establish those properties.

rows.label: Thirty days local
rows.how: Before indexes, encryption overhead and spare capacity

rows.label: Summary payload
rows.how: About 690 times less payload, still sensitive

steps.q: The service itself decrypts uploaded notes to build an ordinary search index. Which privacy claim is accurate?
choices: Content is encrypted in transit and storage, but readable by the service
Content is end-to-end encrypted because only the indexing worker has the key
Content is hidden from the service if the worker discards plaintext after indexing
steps.why: Temporary or restricted server access is still plaintext access within the service trust boundary.

steps.q: Can we keep server search and claim the service cannot read notes? Follow-up: what does the first version offer?
checklist: Keep note keys and plaintext search indexes on authorized devices
Name timing and size leakage and the loss of ordinary server search
Describe authenticated enrollment and a user-held recovery secret
steps.model: Ordinary server plaintext indexing contradicts that claim. In the first version, devices encrypt notes with a random collection key and search a local plaintext index. An existing authorized device authenticates enrollment and wraps the collection key for the new device. A user-held recovery secret can unwrap a separately stored encrypted key backup; the server never receives that secret. Losing every device and the recovery secret means losing access. Timing and sizes still leak metadata. If server plaintext processing is required, I would change the trust claim explicitly.

steps.title: Keys and deletion are workflows
steps.text: Use authenticated encryption, unique nonces under a key and well-reviewed libraries. Wrap per-user or per-collection data keys with keys kept in the device's protected key store. Authenticate new devices, provide revocation and explain recovery before a device is lost. Routine wrapping-key rotation can rewrap data keys. If a wrapping key was compromised, an attacker may already have unwrapped data keys, so rewrapping alone cannot restore confidentiality. Rotate affected data keys and re-encrypt future content as needed; already copied plaintext cannot be recalled. Revocation cannot erase plaintext already copied by an old device. Deletion covers active rows, object versions, indexes, caches, exports and backups. Track a deletion job through each store and prove completion with a receipt and a restore test. Backup expiry may bound final deletion. Cryptographic erasure works only if every usable copy of the relevant key is gone. Be precise about evidence and residual limits instead of promising an impossible universal proof.

steps.q: Every authorized device is lost. The service holds no content recovery secret. What could still restore encrypted notes?
choices: A password reset plus a fresh device-generated content key
A recovery secret the user saved before the loss
Rewrapping the stored ciphertext with a new server metadata key
steps.why: A new key cannot decrypt old ciphertext. Recovery needs an existing content key or a secret that can unwrap it.

steps.q: The customer asks for proof of deletion. What can we actually prove? Follow-up: a backup is restored next week.
checklist: Inventory object versions, indexes, backups and usable key copies
State per-store deletion evidence and backup expiry deadlines
Reapply the deletion ledger before a restored backup serves requests
steps.model: I can provide evidence that our managed stores processed a deletion, with per-store receipts, object-version checks and key-lifecycle records. I cannot prove an endpoint never copied plaintext. Restores must reapply a deletion ledger before serving data, or the backup must already be unreadable through complete key erasure. I would state when backups expire and test a restore against that promise. Keeping the evidence minimal avoids creating a new archive of the deleted content.

steps.q: Active rows are deleted, but retained backups still contain decryptable copies. Which receipt is accurate?
choices: Deletion is complete because backups are not part of the live service
Deletion is complete once the current wrapping key is rotated
Active deletion is verified; backup expiry and restore suppression remain tracked
steps.why: Retained keys may still decrypt backups after rotation. Receipts must state the remaining backup boundary and deadline.

takeaway: Choose what leaves the device, who holds keys and how deletion finishes before collecting data.

title: How metrics systems work
summary: Series count, replication and query work decide the size of a metrics platform.

steps.title: One new label fills memory
steps.text: A latency metric has labels for service, route, region and status. Someone adds request_id. Suddenly almost every request creates a new series. The sample rate did not change much, but the series metadata and index did. In a metrics system, each distinct metric name and label set identifies a time series.

steps.title: The ingest and storage path
steps.text: Authenticate a tenant before accepting writes. Validate label counts, sizes and allowed dimensions. One design sends each series to a replicated ingester set with a WAL. Another appends to a replicated durable log first, then lets ingesters consume it. Mimir supports classic ingester replication and an ingest-storage architecture with Kafka-backed durability; do not assume both acknowledge at the same boundary. Prometheus alone uses a local TSDB and WAL, not this distributed ring. Recent samples become compressed immutable blocks; a distributed backend can upload them to object storage. Indexes select series and blocks. Compaction rewrites blocks, while retention removes expired data. Downsampling is an optional separate policy, not an automatic Mimir or Prometheus retention feature. Preserve count and sum for combined averages, and use semantics-aware summaries for counters and histograms.

steps.title: Worked example: cardinality and bytes
steps.text: Suppose 100 services each expose 20 routes in 3 regions with 5 status classes. If all combinations exist, one metric has 30,000 series. Sampling every 15 seconds gives 2,000 samples/s. At the catalog's roughly 1.5 compressed bytes/sample, 15 days hold about 3.89 GB of sample payload before replication, indexes and metadata. Multiplying by a million possible request ids can make the upper bound enormous, though actual cardinality depends on observed combinations. At an assumed 2 KB of active metadata per series, even 10 million active series need about 20 GB before samples. This example is not a simulated memory allocation.

steps.q: Samples/s stays fixed, but a new user-id label creates many short-lived series. Why can memory rise?
choices: Per-series metadata and churn grow independently of sample count
The same sample count must consume the same memory after compression
Only historical object storage grows; active memory depends solely on samples/s
steps.why: Samples and active-series state are separate costs. Churn also creates WAL and index work.

steps.q: Why does the bill rise when the sample count barely changes? Follow-up: which tenant limit do you add first?
checklist: Separate samples/s, active-series count and new-series rate
Calculate 20 GB for ten million series at assumed 2 KB each
Cap active series first, then churn, and expose rejection reasons
steps.model: I would look at active series and new-series rate as well as samples/s. A request id can turn reused series into short-lived ones, increasing metadata, index and WAL work. If active metadata is about 2 KB, ten million series already need about 20 GB before sample buffers. For this memory incident I would cap active series first, then bound new-series rate to control churn. I would return a rejection reason and show quota usage. Query scanned work needs separate limits. One universal requests/s limit cannot represent these costs.

steps.title: Do not let queries starve writes
steps.text: A query frontend splits long time ranges into bounded pieces and schedules them across workers. Each worker selects relevant blocks and series, then merges partial results. Cache historical results with tenant, authorization scope and full query semantics in the key. Immutable blocks do not guarantee immutable results: late data, deletions, lookback windows and query evaluation times can change them. Use a stable-data cutoff, invalidation or a bounded TTL. Fresh ranges need a short TTL or an explicit cutoff. Limit query concurrency, scanned bytes, range length, samples and wall time per tenant, independently of ingest limits. Limit active series, new-series rate and samples/s on writes. Fair queues let a small tenant make progress beside an expensive scan. Replication multiplies recent write work; object storage durability is a separate mechanism. Measure both query p99 and data freshness, since acknowledging buffered writes is not the same as making them queryable.

steps.q: One window has 10 requests averaging 10 ms; another has 90 averaging 100 ms. What is the combined mean?
choices: 55 ms, averaging the two window means
100 ms, using the larger window's mean for the whole period
91 ms, using total duration divided by total count
steps.why: (10 × 10 + 90 × 100) ÷ 100 = 91 ms. Keep sum and count when combining unequal windows.

steps.q: Why keep a durable recent-write log and object blocks? Follow-up: an ingester dies before its next flush.
checklist: Recover accepted samples not yet published in verified object blocks
State log fsync and host or zone loss guarantees at acknowledgement
Measure replay time and query visibility lag separately
steps.model: Blocks arrive after ingestion, so accepted samples still need a durable recovery source until upload is complete and verified. That can be replicated ingester WALs or a separate replicated ingest log. I would state whether acknowledgement waits for fsync and which host or zone failures it survives. A WAL append alone may only reach an operating-system buffer. Recovery replays from a checkpoint without duplicating logical samples. I would measure replay time and query visibility separately: a sample can be durable before an ingester has consumed it.

steps.q: A tenant stays under ingest quotas but launches 100 wide queries. Which control bounds its read-side work?
choices: A smaller active-series quota on newly ingested data alone
Per-tenant query concurrency, scanned work and execution deadlines
A global HTTP rate limit that counts each query as one request
steps.why: A wide query can cost far more than one write or lookup. Bound expensive work and schedule it fairly.

takeaway: Budget series, samples, replicated bytes and scanned query work separately.

title: Logs and traces
summary: Keep enough evidence to explain failures without indexing or retaining everything.

steps.title: An error chart rises, but why?
steps.text: Checkout errors climb at 09:00. A metric identifies the service and time range. A linked trace shows a slow inventory call, and logs for that trace explain a timeout. Metrics summarize, traces connect causally related spans, and logs preserve detailed events. Collecting all three without useful links only creates three separate search problems.

steps.title: Index a little or index the words
steps.text: A label-indexed log store maps bounded labels and time ranges to compressed chunks in object storage. It then scans selected chunks for words. Cheap ingestion and a small index suit known service and time filters; broad text searches may read many bytes. A full-text index maps words to matching records and speeds some searches, at the cost of index writes, storage and memory. Keep request ids as fields or structured metadata rather than creating millions of streams. Neither approach excuses access control or secret removal before export. Traces group spans by trace id and parent relationships; clock skew can distort cross-host placement and inferred latency. Measure a local span duration with a monotonic clock where possible; parent and link identities express relationships that wall-clock order cannot prove.

steps.title: Worked example: sampling trade-offs
steps.text: Assume 10,000 traces/s, 20 spans/trace and 500 bytes/span before compression. Raw spans are about 100 MB/s or 8.64 TB/day. A 10% head sample keeps about 0.864 TB/day if chosen consistently for the whole trace. It cannot know that a later span will fail. Tail sampling waits for spans, then selects errors, slow traces and a baseline. For a sizing example, assume spans remain buffered for an average of 30 seconds. At this load that is roughly 3 GB of raw spans, before metadata and replicas. A 30-second decision timer alone does not establish average residence time: span arrival times, decision caches and late spans change memory use. Late or missing spans and collector failure can still yield incomplete traces. The sim does not implement sampling or trace assembly, so these are explicit worked assumptions.

rows.label: Illustrative tail buffer
rows.how: 100 MB/s × assumed 30 s average residence, before overhead and copies

steps.q: A trace fails at its last span. A consistent uniform 10% head sampler is independent of outcome. What can it promise?
choices: Retention of the failed trace because the last span can revise the head decision
About a 10% chance of retaining that trace, subject to delivery loss
A 10% chance per span, giving almost every failed trace at least one span
steps.why: Head selection happens before the outcome and should propagate one trace decision, rather than independently sampling spans.

steps.q: Why not index every log word? Follow-up: support needs broad searches once a week.
checklist: Compare frequent narrow searches with the cost of indexing every word
Budget the weekly broad search as a bounded scan or short indexed tier
Enforce tenant authorization, redaction and retention on both paths
steps.model: A full-text index may be worth it if arbitrary searches are central to the product. If most users know the service and time, a label index plus chunk scans can spend much less on continuous indexing. I would measure scanned bytes and weekly search latency, then offer a bounded asynchronous scan or a shorter indexed retention tier for support. Tenant isolation, redaction and deadlines apply to either path. The choice depends on query frequency and acceptable waiting, not a universal winner.

steps.title: Retain by value
steps.text: Route all spans of a trace to the same tail decision group, bound memory and define the late-span policy. Head sampling protects the collector and network earlier; tail sampling can retain more failures but must first receive the data. A metric exemplar stores a link to a selected trace, not an entire label dimension. Propagate trace context across queues and mark asynchronous links where a parent-child tree is misleading. Retain security events and evidence of rare failures longer than routine debug output, under explicit policy. Record inclusion probabilities when they are known. A complex tail policy may not provide usable unbiased weights, so do not assume a configured baseline percentage corrects every sampled count. Protect the underlying user SLI from bias: count all eligible requests in metrics even if only some traces survive.

steps.q: Most log searches specify a service and narrow time range. Which design avoids a continuous full-text indexing bill?
choices: Index bounded stream labels and scan the selected chunks
Index request ids as stream labels to narrow every search
Index every token but reduce chunk compression to offset the write cost
steps.why: Bounded labels and time reduce candidate chunks. Request-id streams grow cardinality; full-text indexing adds ongoing work.

steps.q: Tail sampling keeps all errors. What could still be missing? Follow-up: the collector restarts halfway through a trace.
checklist: Name upstream drops, late spans and buffer eviction as missing evidence
Explain what collector restart loses without durable replay
Use independent eligible-request counters for the error-rate SLI
steps.model: It can keep all errors only among traces it receives and recognizes within its policy. Head-dropped spans, network loss, late spans or buffer eviction can hide the error. A collector restart loses in-memory assembly unless we provide durable buffering and replay. I would define these limits, route trace ids consistently, monitor sampling drops and keep an unbiased request counter outside the sampled trace path. Retaining an error trace is evidence, not proof that every error was observed.

steps.q: Tail sampling keeps errors preferentially, and inclusion probabilities are unknown. What should supply the error-rate SLI?
choices: Retained error traces divided by all retained traces
Retained errors divided by the configured baseline sample fraction
Complete eligible-request counters measured independently
steps.why: Outcome-dependent retention changes the denominator. A baseline fraction alone does not describe every trace's inclusion probability.

takeaway: Choose the index and sampling policy from the questions people need to answer.

title: SLOs and error budgets
summary: Turn a user promise into a budget and an actionable alert.

steps.title: The green dashboard nobody trusts
steps.text: Servers are healthy, but one in fifty checkout attempts times out. CPU is green because requests are waiting on a dependency. Start with an SLI, a measured user outcome: the fraction of eligible checkout attempts that finish successfully within two seconds. An SLO is its target over a named window. Define which attempts count, where they are measured and which failures are excluded before choosing a percentage.

steps.title: A budget for decisions
steps.text: For a 99.9% success SLO, the allowed bad fraction is 0.1%. At a steady 1,000 requests/s over 30 days, there are about 2.592 billion requests and a budget of 2.592 million bad requests. A request-based budget is not automatically 43.2 minutes of downtime: that equivalence assumes uniform traffic and total failure during those minutes. Use remaining budget to choose between feature work and reliability work. A shared policy might pause risky launches when budget is exhausted while still allowing repairs. Agree the policy with the people who own releases; a graph alone cannot make that decision.

steps.title: Worked example: burn rate
steps.text: Burn rate is observed bad fraction divided by allowed bad fraction. At 1.44% failures against a 99.9% target, burn is 14.4. One hour at that rate uses about 14.4/720 = 2% of a 30-day budget under steady traffic. An example fast page requires burn above 14.4 in both the last hour and the last five minutes. The long window establishes impact; the short window checks that it is still happening. A slower page might require burn above 6 in both six hours and thirty minutes. Six hours at burn 6 uses about 5% of the budget. These are starting policies with worked assumptions, not universal thresholds or a simulated alert evaluator.

steps.q: The fast alert requires burn above 14.4 in both windows. The hour shows 20 and five minutes shows 0.2. Does this rule fire?
choices: Yes; the long window has already established budget impact
No; its recent window is below the threshold
Yes; averaging the two windows preserves the long-window breach
steps.why: The rule uses AND. A healthy recent window stops this fast alert after recovery; other alert policies are evaluated separately.

steps.q: Why is 99.99% not automatically the right target? Follow-up: product says every failure matters.
checklist: Define an eligible user outcome and the harm of missing it
Show that 99.99% permits one tenth the failures of 99.9%
Assign reliability work and release policy to important user cohorts
steps.model: Every failure can matter without making every operation equally critical. Moving from 99.9% to 99.99% reduces the allowed bad fraction tenfold. I would identify the journeys where that cost is justified, separate critical cohorts, and estimate the redundancy and on-call work required. The target should lead to a funded decision policy. A promise the team cannot sustain encourages exclusions and noisy pages rather than better user outcomes.

steps.title: Make a page worth answering
steps.text: Combine each pair with AND, then combine fast and slow policies with OR. Deduplicate related pages and attach an owner, dashboard and runbook. Recovered short windows should stop paging even if a long window still contains an old incident. Low-traffic services need special handling: a handful of failures can produce unstable percentages, so consider minimum event counts, synthetic checks and user-impact judgement. Avoid hiding a critical small population in a global average; define important cohorts. Keep all eligible-request counters independent of biased trace sampling. Review pages that needed no action and incidents that produced no page. Alert fatigue is a design failure with a human cost.

steps.q: A 99.9% SLO sees 0.6% bad requests. What is its burn rate?
steps.why: 0.006 ÷ 0.001 = 6. Use the allowed bad fraction, not the success target.

steps.q: Why use two windows instead of paging on every error spike? Follow-up: could that miss a short severe outage?
checklist: Explain long-window impact and short-window confirmation
Calculate budget use and fast-alert detection delay
Define a separate fast path if severe harm requires it
steps.model: A long window avoids paging on tiny blips, and a short window confirms the problem is current. At burn 14.4, an hour spends roughly 2% of a steady 30-day budget. At steady traffic, a 100% outage burns at 1,000, so it can push a previously healthy one-hour average above 14.4 in about 52 seconds. The rule does not wait a full hour to act. A shorter total outage may deserve an independent synthetic or availability fast path if its user harm is high. I would test detection delay on real incident shapes, keep pages deduplicated and make every page lead to an action. Multi-window rules are a tool, not a reason to ignore severe brief failures.

steps.q: A low-traffic service has ten requests and one failure. Which alert design accounts for the small denominator?
choices: Use user impact, event counts and independent synthetic checks
Page on the same percentage-only threshold used for a million-request service
Require a large minimum count for every alert, even a complete outage
steps.why: A ratio alone can be noisy. A blanket event minimum can also hide a severe low-volume outage.

takeaway: Choose a measurable user promise, then page when its budget is being spent fast enough to need action.

title: Many customers on one system
summary: Fairness and failure boundaries matter as much as total capacity.

steps.title: One customer ruins everyone's morning
steps.text: A shared analytics service has plenty of average capacity. One customer submits a thousand broad queries and fills the worker queue. A small customer's one quick query waits behind them. Fleet capacity is not a promise of fair access. Tenant identity must follow work through admission, queues, caches and storage.

steps.title: Budget work at every scarce resource
steps.text: Set per-tenant rate, concurrency, queue-depth and work limits. Requests/s alone misses the difference between one key lookup and a terabyte scan. Weighted fair queueing or deficit round robin can reserve progress for active tenants while lending unused capacity. Bound queue age and propagate cancellation so abandoned queries stop consuming resources. Reject overload with clear reasons and retry guidance. Distinguish admitted traffic from rejected demand in the SLI and contract so quotas cannot hide a broken service. A tenant with many API keys must not escape an account-level limit.

steps.title: Worked example: cells and overlap
steps.text: Divide 2,000 tenants evenly across 20 cells. A cell owns its ingress, workers and data path, so one cell failure reaches about 100 tenants, or 5% of tenant count, under even placement. It need not represent 5% of requests or revenue. That bound is false if all cells need one shared database to serve requests. Shuffle sharding instead assigns each tenant a small subset of a larger worker pool. Choosing 2 of 10 workers yields 45 possible pairs. Under uniform independent assignment, two tenants have a 1/45 chance of the same pair, but a 17/45 chance of sharing at least one worker. Partial overlap still matters. The sim can model a noisy-neighbour event, but not this assignment distribution.

steps.q: One tenant scans 1 TB per query while another reads one key. Which policy bounds the first tenant's use of shared workers?
choices: Identical per-tenant requests/s limits with one shared FIFO
Per-tenant concurrency and scan budgets with fair scheduling
A larger global FIFO sized to absorb the scan burst
steps.why: Equal request counts can represent very different resource use. FIFO waiting does not reserve progress for another tenant.

steps.q: Why not just add more workers for the noisy tenant? Follow-up: queries keep getting wider.
checklist: Explain why extra workers alone cannot bound ever-wider scans
Limit scan work, concurrency and queue age, and cancel expired work
Offer funded quota increases or a dedicated cell for sustained demand
steps.model: Extra workers buy time, but unbounded scans can consume them too. I would cap concurrency and estimated or observed scan work, schedule fairly, cancel expired work and give explicit rejection feedback. A customer with sustained justified demand can buy a larger quota or a dedicated cell. I would protect the service promised to smaller tenants while measuring both admitted success and demand rejected by policy.

steps.title: Trace the actual blast radius
steps.text: Cells provide a concrete failure boundary only if their critical data, queues and deployment controls respect it. A shared control plane can provision cells without sitting on every request path. Cache keys and authorization must include the tenant; fairness is useless if data leaks. Test a runaway query, full disk, bad deployment and control-plane outage. List which tenants each event can reach, including shared identity, DNS and key services. Larger tenants may need dedicated cells or higher priced quotas. More isolation costs idle headroom, duplicated operations and migration work. Make that cost visible rather than selling unlimited capacity on a shared pool.

steps.q: Twenty cells synchronously use one shared database for every query. What can that database's outage affect?
choices: Only one cell because each has its own worker pool
At most the tenants assigned to the busiest cell
Every cell that needs it
steps.why: Separate workers do not isolate a critical shared data dependency.

steps.q: You claim a cell failure reaches only 5%. Prove it. Follow-up: the key service fails.
checklist: Map one twentieth of tenants to an independent cell data path
Identify shared key, identity and deployment dependencies
Test a key-service outage and qualify the 5% tenant-count claim
steps.model: That number assumes even tenant placement and a failure contained to one of twenty cells. I would inventory each critical dependency and trace affected tenants. If every request synchronously needs one key service, its outage may reach everyone, so the 5% claim does not apply. Caching valid key material safely, regional redundancy or cell-local services may reduce that reach, but each needs a security and expiry policy. I would verify with failure tests, not a box boundary.

steps.q: Two tenants independently choose uniform unordered pairs from ten workers. What is their chance of any shared worker?
choices: 17/45; only 1/45 is an identical pair
1/45; overlap requires choosing the same pair
16/45; count the pairs sharing exactly one worker
steps.why: Of 45 pairs, 28 avoid both workers. The other 17 include 16 single overlaps and one identical pair.

takeaway: Limit work per tenant and trace every shared dependency before claiming a small blast radius.

title: How to lead a design interview
summary: Use the hour to make decisions, test assumptions and invite useful disagreement.

steps.title: The prompt is only five words
steps.text: You are asked to design a notification service. You could spend the hour drawing queues, but nobody has said whether messages are promotional emails or urgent medical alerts. Leading the discussion starts by turning a vague noun into a user journey and a few testable promises. State a provisional scope and ask which assumption would most change the design.

steps.title: A flexible plan for sixty minutes
steps.text: Use roughly 0 to 8 minutes for users, scope, exclusions and failure promises. Spend 8 to 15 on traffic, payload and storage estimates. Use 15 to 30 to draw one complete request path and explain the data model. Spend 30 to 47 on the hardest constraint: a hot key, a partial failure, consistency or recovery. Use 47 to 55 to test failures, cost and operations, and leave 55 to 60 to summarize decisions and open questions. These are checkpoints, not a script. If a requirement reveals a major risk, move the depth earlier and say why.

steps.title: Worked example: choose the deep question
steps.text: Assume 10 million users receive 3 notifications/day. That is 30 million/day, or about 347/s average. With a 10 times burst, plan about 3,470/s. At an assumed 1 KB payload, raw events add about 30 GB/day, before replicas and delivery attempts. If the provider admits only 2,000/s, an extra app fleet cannot erase the downstream limit. Using the unrounded burst rate of about 3,472/s, a five-minute burst creates about 441,667 queued notifications if service stays at 2,000/s. That calculation suggests going deep on admission, deadlines and recovery. It is a worked design exercise, not a sim run.

rows.label: Five-minute backlog
rows.how: (30 million ÷ 86,400 × 10 - 2,000)/s × 300 s; round at the end

steps.q: Eight minutes in, the delivery deadline is still unknown. Which next step best resolves the queue policy?
choices: Choose an unbounded durable queue now and settle delivery timing later
Agree deadlines by message class before choosing buffering and expiry
Use the provider's acknowledgement latency as the delivery deadline
steps.why: Acceptance latency does not define user delivery. The deadline determines whether buffering, expiry or admission is acceptable.

steps.q: Why did you spend time on numbers before choosing services? Follow-up: your traffic estimate is wrong by ten times.
checklist: Compare assumed arrival rates with the provider ceiling and deadline
Calculate how the design changes across a tenfold traffic range
Label assumed inputs and name the measurement that could change the design
steps.model: With 30 million events/day, average traffic is about 347/s and the assumed tenfold burst is about 3,472/s. A 2,000/s provider is already the peak bottleneck. If the estimate is ten times lower, the roughly 347/s peak fits; ten times higher gives about 34,722/s, where buffering and quotas dominate. I would ask how long delivery may wait and verify sustained account quotas. Those measurements determine whether admission, another provider or a narrower promise is needed. Extra app servers cannot raise a downstream ceiling.

steps.title: Make the reasoning visible
steps.text: Say which numbers are assumptions and which would come from measurement. Explain one simple design before alternatives. Tie each component to a requirement and name what happens on failure. Ask for pushback on a concrete decision: is delayed delivery acceptable for this message class? If you do not know a provider limit, give a plausible range, show how the design changes across it and name the measurement needed. Do not invent certainty. End with the key invariant, the bottleneck, the cost driver and one unresolved risk. A good discussion can disagree with your choice because it can see why you made it.

steps.q: The provider limit is unknown and could change the design. What supports the next decision?
choices: Use the published maximum as sustained account capacity without verification
Size only the average rate and defer provider limits until after launch
State a plausible range, test both ends and name the needed measurement
steps.why: A published maximum may not be an account's safe sustained capacity. Test whether the uncertainty changes admission or buffering.

steps.q: I disagree with your choice of deep dive. How do you respond? Follow-up: there are only fifteen minutes left.
checklist: Tie the current deep dive to the delivery promise at risk
Ask which competing failure could invalidate the design sooner
Allocate the last fifteen minutes and reserve time to record decisions
steps.model: I chose provider admission because it may break the delivery deadline even when our app has spare capacity. I would ask which requirement the alternative deep dive puts at greater risk. If it changes the main design, I would switch. With fifteen minutes left, I would propose ten minutes on that failure, three on recovery and operations, and two to record decisions and unresolved risks. I would keep the rest at a stated high level so we leave with a design we can assess.

steps.q: Ten minutes remain. Provider overload may violate delivery deadlines; three other topics are unexplored. How should you use the time?
choices: Test that bottleneck and its failure policy, then record the remaining risks
Give each of the four topics equal time regardless of user impact
Add a second provider without checking its quota or duplicate-delivery behavior
steps.why: Use remaining depth to test the constraint most likely to invalidate the user promise. Extra providers need their own failure analysis.

takeaway: Lead with a user promise, make assumptions testable and spend depth where it can change the design.

title: The simplest thing that works
summary: Include people, failure recovery and future triggers in the cost of a design.

steps.title: Six services for a quiet product
steps.text: A team with four engineers proposes six services and a sharded database for a product serving 200 requests/s. Each service needs deployment, dashboards, contracts and someone to answer its pages. The diagram scales on paper, but the team is now the scarce resource. Simplicity means the fewest moving parts that meet the actual requirements, with a path to change.

steps.title: Put build and buy on the same horizon
steps.text: Compare three-year total cost, including engineering, infrastructure, support, upgrades, incidents, compliance work, egress and migration out. List which costs are assumptions. A managed service can charge more per unit and still save months of work. Building can win when control, unusual scale, residency or product differentiation justifies ownership. Check contracts, exit formats and operating limits before deciding. A modular service with a clear internal boundary may preserve future choices without a network boundary today. Do not shard just because the data may grow; measure write headroom, index size, maintenance time and recovery time first.

steps.title: Worked example: three years
steps.text: Assume loaded engineering cost of $180,000 per engineer-year. Building a specialized queue needs 0.5 engineer for year one and 0.2 for each of years two and three: 0.9 engineer-years, or $162,000. Add $2,000/month infrastructure for 36 months: $72,000. Total is about $234,000. Buying at $4,000/month costs $144,000. Add 0.1 engineer-year integration and 0.05/year operations for three years: $45,000, total $189,000. Buying is about $45,000 cheaper under these assumptions. A 50% vendor price rise applying to all 36 months would add $72,000 and reverse the result unless other costs change. This is a sensitivity exercise, not catalog pricing.

steps.q: A managed service costs twice the raw VMs. What is needed before comparing build and buy?
choices: VM costs plus initial implementation effort, excluding ongoing operations
A common ownership horizon including people, recovery and exit costs
Vendor fees versus VM cost after assuming equal maintenance effort
steps.why: Operating effort can differ substantially. Include it explicitly along with the guarantees each option meets.

steps.q: Your design seems too simple for year two. Follow-up: traffic grows tenfold.
checklist: Test 200 requests/s and the 2,000/s growth case with the actual write mix
Set a measured ceiling and allow time to migrate before reaching it
Include tested backups, restore targets and authorization initially
steps.model: I would show today's tested capacity, the tenfold case and where the first ceiling lies. At 200 requests/s, tenfold traffic is 2,000/s, which may still fit one well-indexed store depending on the write mix. I would avoid promising that without a benchmark. Stable keys, modular boundaries and exportable data leave room for a later split. I would fund the migration before measured headroom or recovery time crosses its trigger, while retaining backups and correctness from day one.

steps.title: A plan with triggers
steps.text: Month one: one deployable service, a transactional store, backups with a restore test, and basic user-outcome monitoring. Month six: add a cache or background queue only if measured latency or workload justifies it; keep the invariant in one place. Year two: split ownership or shard when an observed ceiling, team boundary or recovery target demands it. Start migration before forecast write utilization crosses the tested safe level or restore time exceeds the recovery objective. Include the time to migrate and verify, so the trigger leaves enough headroom. Keep identifiers, APIs and export paths ready for change. Simpler is not an excuse to omit durability, authorization or a viable rollback. The minimum design must still satisfy every binding requirement.

steps.q: One store meets tested peak and recovery targets. Which evidence most directly justifies planning a shard migration?
choices: The dataset doubled even though its tested working set and write load remain safe
Adding stateless API replicas requires adding the same number of database shards
Forecast headroom or restore time will cross a tested limit before migration can finish
steps.why: Use a measured ceiling and migration lead time. Data growth or API replica count alone does not establish a need to shard.

steps.q: Buying is cheaper in your table. Why might we still build? Follow-up: who owns it after launch?
checklist: Name a residency rule or missing guarantee that rules out the cheaper vendor
Assign a team capacity for upgrades, incidents and succession
Recalculate operating effort, migration-out cost and remaining risk
steps.model: A hard residency rule, a missing guarantee or a core differentiating feature could rule out that vendor. I would make the requirement explicit and revise the comparison, including the cost of meeting it ourselves. A named team needs capacity for upgrades, incidents and succession after the original authors leave. If we cannot staff that ownership, a more expensive supported option or a narrower product may be the responsible decision.

steps.q: A single service has backups but has never tested a restore. What is still unproven?
choices: Whether it can recover correct data within its recovery targets
Nothing, if every backup job reports success
Only recovery speed; a completed backup guarantees correct restoration
steps.why: Backup success does not establish restore correctness or duration. Test both against the recovery promise.

takeaway: Choose the smallest design that meets the promise, and attach measured triggers to future complexity.

title: Changing a running system
summary: A safe migration preserves compatibility through the whole rollback window.

steps.title: The new column is ready, but old apps are not
steps.text: You want to replace a free-text address with structured fields. Web code can update today, but mobile clients will keep sending the old shape for months. A migration is a period when multiple schemas and code versions coexist. A deployment that works only after every client updates is not a rollout plan.

steps.title: Expand, move, contract
steps.text: Expand by adding compatible fields and readers before removing anything. Establish one authoritative write path. If you must dual write, record a durable intent or use a transactional outbox or change-data capture so a committed source change can eventually reach the target after partial failure. This does not make both stores update atomically. Make replay idempotent and versioned so an old backfill cannot overwrite a fresh write. Backfill in bounded batches with checkpoints, throttling and reconciliation. Shadow reads compare results without changing user responses; redact sensitive differences. Cut over a small cohort, then increase gradually while watching correctness and SLOs. Contract by deleting the old path only after clients, replay, backups and the rollback window no longer require it.

steps.title: Worked example: how long it takes
steps.text: A table has 500 million rows. At a safe 5,000 rows/s, a backfill alone takes 100,000 seconds, or about 27.8 hours. At 500 bytes/row that is about 250 GB of logical data before indexes and replicas. Retries, live changes and reconciliation make the real operation longer. If writes continue at 2,000/s and the change consumer handles 5,000/s, a backlog of 30 million changes drains at 3,000/s, about 2.8 hours. A canary might start at 1%, then 5%, 25% and all eligible traffic, but percentages do not replace minimum observation time or coverage of large tenants. The sim does not execute schema changes row by row.

rows.label: Logical copied bytes
rows.how: 500 million × 500 B, before index and replication

steps.q: A backfill reads version 5, then a live write creates version 6. What prevents the delayed copy from regressing the target?
choices: A unique backfill job id used for deduplication
An atomic version check, or snapshot-and-log replay ordered through cutover
A later ingestion timestamp on whichever copy arrives last
steps.why: Deduplication prevents repeated application of one job. Version checks or correctly ordered replay also prevent stale overwrite.

steps.q: Why not write to both databases in the request handler? Follow-up: the first write succeeds and the second times out.
checklist: Treat a timed-out second write as an unknown outcome
Atomically capture source changes and replay versioned target writes
Name one write authority and compare both stores before cutover
steps.model: Two independent writes leave an ambiguous state. I would keep one authority and atomically record its change with an outbox or capture its committed log. The target applies versioned changes idempotently and exposes lag. A timeout is reconciled rather than treated as proof of failure. During cutover I would compare the stores and keep a documented source of truth. A second successful API reply alone does not prove the databases contain the same state.

steps.title: Rollback is a data decision
steps.text: Before cutover, define which versions can read new writes and what happens to writes accepted during the canary. A code rollback is unsafe if the old code cannot understand the new representation. Preserve compatible writes or provide a tested reverse transform where possible. Watch mismatch rate, lag, p99, lock time and support signals with stop thresholds. Agree ownership with application and data teams, on-call, security and product; support needs user-facing failure states. Reserve time for review, a full backfill, verification, staged traffic, a stable rollback period and old-client deprecation. Calendar time can be weeks even when copying bytes takes a day.

steps.q: A canary writes a new enum that old code cannot parse. What must be addressed before reverting the binary?
choices: Only restore the old configuration before deploying the old binary
Only stop new canary traffic; its committed data is unaffected by rollback
Preserve old-readable data or test a recovery transform for the new writes
steps.why: New data survives the deployment. Reverting code alone leaves unreadable rows in place.

steps.q: The backfill takes one day. Why did you ask for three weeks? Follow-up: who can stop the rollout?
checklist: Separate copy time from live-write catch-up and verification
Require representative canaries and a tested rollback window
Name the rollout lead and concrete stop thresholds
steps.model: The copy floor excludes throttling, catching live changes, verifying results, representative canaries and a rollback window. Old clients and backup restores may need the old schema longer. I would give application, data and on-call owners shared stop criteria such as mismatch rate, replication lag or p99 regression, with one named rollout lead. For example, stop on any unexplained lost address field, lag beyond the allowed catch-up window, or p99 above the agreed target; choose thresholds from this workload rather than copying them blindly. Product and support need to agree the user states and deprecation deadline. We can shorten the calendar only by explicitly changing that evidence or compatibility requirement.

steps.q: A 1% canary passes for thirty seconds on a low-volume service. What evidence is still missing?
choices: Representative paths and tenants observed long enough to exercise delayed work
A 25% canary for the same thirty seconds, regardless of request mix
A successful deployment health check in every zone
steps.why: More traffic or healthy processes alone can miss rare paths, scheduled jobs and delayed correctness failures.

takeaway: Migrate through compatible states and prove that rollback still understands the data.

title: Designs that other teams must live with
summary: A boundary is a contract and an operating responsibility, not just a box.

steps.title: A shared API changes under three teams
steps.text: Your team renames a response field. The website updates, but a billing job and an old mobile client fail overnight. The data shape was an informal contract even though nobody wrote it down. A design crosses team boundaries whenever another team must depend on its behavior, availability or change schedule.

steps.title: Put authority with an owner
steps.text: Choose boundaries around coherent data and invariants, access patterns and the teams able to operate them. Name the authoritative writer and the on-call owner for each dataset and API. Shared ownership without a decision rule can mean nobody owns recovery. Too many tiny services spread a single invariant across network calls; a huge shared service can make every change a negotiation. Use an internal module when it preserves cohesion without requiring independent deployment. A service boundary earns its cost when it creates useful autonomy, security or scaling isolation. Include dashboards, runbooks and dependency failure behavior in the contract.

steps.title: Worked example: the on-call bill
steps.text: Assume four services each produce two actionable pages a week, and each page consumes 45 minutes including follow-up. That is eight pages and six hours/week, or about 312 hours/year. If only three engineers can operate the stack, those pages and recovery work constrain delivery. Combining services will not automatically remove pages; eliminating duplicated failure paths or clarifying ownership might. For an API deprecation with 200 callers, suppose 180 migrate in month one. The last 20 may include the least observable batch jobs. Count actual endpoint use and caller identity rather than declaring 90% migration complete enough. This is an operating model, not a simulated page count.

rows.label: Remaining callers
rows.how: 200 - 180; risk depends on which callers remain

steps.q: Three teams write one table and each assumes another owns recovery. What must their contract establish?
choices: A shared on-call channel with no authority to settle conflicting writes
Allowed writers, invariant enforcement, recovery owner and change rules
One API schema while leaving direct table writes unrestricted
steps.why: A communication channel and schema are useful, but do not assign data authority or recovery decisions.

steps.q: Where would you split this service? Follow-up: another team needs to change independently.
checklist: Map writes that must commit together and assign their authority
Explain whether an API boundary can preserve the invariant
Assign versioning, dependency-failure behavior and recovery ownership
steps.model: I would first map the writes that must commit together and who can operate them. A separate team can own a coherent capability through an API without directly mutating another team's tables. If that boundary splits an invariant, we need a redesigned workflow or must keep the transaction together. I would document data authority, versioning, failure behavior and on-call before treating independent deployment as a benefit. A module boundary may be enough until the operating case is clear.

steps.title: Write a document people can disagree with
steps.text: Start with the problem, user promises, explicit non-goals and measured constraints. Show one request path, data ownership and the key invariant. Record alternatives and why they lost, then failures, costs, security boundaries, rollout and open questions. Ask reviewers to challenge a specific decision. API contracts need field semantics, error states, idempotency, rate limits and compatibility rules; data contracts need schema, meaning, freshness and deletion behavior. Prefer additive changes, tolerant readers where safe and explicit versions for incompatible meaning. Publish deprecation dates, contact owners, instrument use, offer a migration path and test old clients. Remove the old endpoint only with evidence that consumers have moved or under an agreed exception policy. An empty dashboard is not proof if an annual job has not run.

steps.q: Ninety percent of callers migrated to a new API. What evidence supports removing the old endpoint?
choices: No calls appeared in the last month, even though annual jobs exist
The website and newest mobile app pass their tests
Remaining callers are identified and migrated or covered by an agreed exception policy
steps.why: Important infrequent or older consumers can remain after the most visible clients migrate.

steps.q: How will you deprecate an API used by teams you do not know? Follow-up: one annual caller never appears in the last month's logs.
checklist: Inventory caller identities through credentials, code and owners
Publish a replacement, support window and owner-tested migration
Account for annual jobs and record exceptions before removal
steps.model: I would inventory consumers from credentials, code references, owners and telemetry, then publish the replacement and a support window. Usage logs are evidence, but a month misses annual jobs. I would ask identified owners to test the replacement and check schedules, run a controlled warning phase and keep an explicit exception owner. Removal needs a decision about the remaining risk. I would record that decision so a future on-call engineer does not have to reconstruct it during an outage.

steps.q: Two actions share a required local transaction invariant and one operating team. What is a reasonable initial boundary?
choices: One cohesive module or service that commits the invariant locally
Separate services with compensations assumed to preserve the same atomic visibility
Separate services that each update their own row without a shared decision
steps.why: Splitting the writes changes failure and visibility semantics. Keep the transaction local unless another requirement warrants redesigning it.

takeaway: Name the invariant, the owner and the compatibility promise before drawing a team boundary.
